W-xgimYNN0M.title: HPE Aruba EP12
tx: In 2002, two engineers in Sunavail, California, bet that wireless would become the main way people connect to
the corporate network. Their company, Aruba Networks, grew into one of the leaders of enterprise Wi-Fi and then
into the core of the networking business of Huelet Packard Enterprise. This is the story of Aruba. controller-based
Wi-Fi, the move into security and network access control, the acquisition by HP, the push into switching, SDWAN
and Sassy, and the combination with Juniper Networks that created a new networking giant will follow six chapters. The founding, the controller
era, the IPO and growth, HP and the intelligent edge, the edge platform, and HPE networking after Juniper.
Aruba Networks was founded in February 2002 in Sunavail by Kir Melcote and Pun
Kaj Mlick. Both were experienced networking engineers and they had seen how slowly enterprise networks were
adapting to laptops and mobile users. At the time, Wi-Fi in businesses was mostly an afterthought. Access points were
installed one by one, each configured on its own, and IT departments worried that wireless was insecure and impossible to
manage at scale. Aruba's founders believed that mobility would change that. Employees would expect to work from anywhere in a building and
eventually from anywhere at all, and the network would need to follow them securely. The company raised venture funding and set out to build a wireless
system designed for large enterprises rather than for homes and small offices.
Aruba's answer was the controller-based architecture. In the early model, every access point was autonomous. Each one
ran its own software, stored its own configuration, and had to be updated separately. So, a large campus could
mean thousands of devices to manage by hand. Aruba used thin access points connected through tunnels to a central
mobility controller. The controller handled configuration security policy, roaming, and radio management for the
whole network. Aruba also built a stateful firewall into the controller, applying policy to each user based on
identity and role rather than just to ports and addresses. It called this identity based networking because the
controller saw every user and every radio. It could also tune channels and power automatically and steer devices to
less crowded access points which mattered more and more as networks grew denser. Cisco which had bought airspace
in 2005 adopted a similar controller model and the two companies became the main rivals in enterprise Wi-Fi for the next decade.
Aruba grew quickly as businesses, universities, and hospitals rolled out Wi-Fi everywhere. In March 2007, it went public on NASDAQ under the ticker RUN.
That year, it also bought Network Chemistry for wireless intrusion detection. In 2008, Aruba acquired
Airwave, whose software could manage wireless and wired networks from many vendors. Airwave became a mainstay of
Aruba's management tools. Then the iPhone and the iPad arrived. Employees began bringing their own phones and
tablets to work and the number of devices on enterprise Wi-Fi exploded.
Aruba was well placed for this bring your own device wave. In 2010, it bought Aelia Networks for outdoor mesh networks
for about $40 million. In 2011, it acquired Aenda Systems, whose technology
became Clear Pass, a policy manager for network access control and device onboarding. Clear Pass let it teams
decide which users and devices could join the network and what they could reach, whether they were employees, guests, or connected medical and
building equipment. In 2013, it bought Meridian for indoor location and mobile apps using Bluetooth beacons. By then,
Aruba's annual revenue was approaching $600 million.
In March 2015, HP announced that it would acquire Aruba Networks for about $3 billion. The deal closed in May 2015.
HP already had a large networking business built partly from its 2010 purchase of 3COM and known as HP Pro
Curve in earlier years, but its wireless products were weaker and Aruba gave it a strong position in campus mobility.
Unusually, HP put Aruba's leaders in charge of its whole campus networking business and kept the Aruba brand. Kir
Melcote went on to lead it for years. In November 2015, HP split into two companies. Aruba became part of Huelet
Packard Enterprise, which later called the business its intelligent edge segment. The idea was that data was increasingly created at the edge in
campuses, branches, factories, and stores, and that the network connecting those places would be central to HPE's strategy.
Inside HPE, Aruba continued to build and buy software especially for security and analytics. In 2016, it acquired Rasa Networks for AIdriven network analytics.
In 2017, it bought Niara, which used machine learning to spot unusual user and device behavior and became Aruba
Introspect. In 2018, Aruba bought Cape Networks, whose small sensors test the network from a user's point of view.
Aruba also moved into data center and campus core switching with a new switch line, Aruba CX, built on a modern
database-driven operating system called OSCX.
And it made Aruba Central its cloud management platform, letting customers manage access points, switches, and gateways from a single cloud service.
Next, Aruba moved beyond the campus to connect branches and secure users anywhere. In September 2020, HPE
acquired Silver Peak, a leader in SDWAN for about $925 million.
Silver Peak's Edge Connect became Aruba's main SDWAN product. That same year, Aruba introduced its edge services
platform, combining AI operations, zero trust security and unified infrastructure across campus, branch,
and data center. In 2023, HPE added two more pieces. Athonet, an Italian
company, brought private 5G and LTE core software and Axis Security bought for
about $470 million brought security service Edge, completing Aruba's sassy offering. Also in 2023, the brand was
renamed HP Aruba Networking, tying it more closely to the parent company, and its services were offered through HPE Green Lake.
Here is how the HPE Aruba networking portfolio fits together. Wi-Fi access points and gateways for campuses and
branches. CX switches from the access layer to the data center and instanton for small businesses. Clear pass for
network access control. Edge connect for SDWAN and SSE. Built on access for secure access to applications from
anywhere. Aruba central for cloud management and AI operations with private 5G from Athonet extending the
same network to factories, warehouses, and outdoor sites.
In January 2024, HPE announced its largest networking deal, the acquisition of Juniper Networks for about $14
billion. The deal faced a long antitrust review. The US Department of Justice
sued to block it in January 2025, arguing it would reduce competition in enterprise Wi-Fi. HPE settled in June
2025, agreeing to sell its instant on business and to license parts of Juniper's Mist AI software. The acquisition closed on July 2, 2025.
Juniper's chief executive Rammy Rahheem became the leader of HPE's combined networking business. The combination
roughly doubled HPE's networking revenue and added Juniper's routing, data center switching, security, and the Mist AI
platform to Aruba's campus and branch products. HPE then began bringing the two product lines together. In 2026, it
announced that the Marvis AI assistant from Mist would come to Aruba Central.
So, customers on either platform would share the same AI operations features.
The goal, according to HPE, is a single self-driving network where AI agents find and fix problems before users
notice them. From the campus to the data center, networking is now one of HPE's most
important businesses. In the third quarter of fiscal 2026, ending in July, HPE's networking segment revenue reached
$2.89 billion, up 75% with an operating margin of 22%.
Networking made up about a quarter of HPE's total revenue. Campus and branch revenue grew 31% to $1.44 billion. Data
center networking more than doubled and routing, mostly from Juniper, reached $788 million.
HPE expects at least $600 million of cost savings from the Juniper combination by fiscal 2028
and the instant on divevestature required by the settlement is still being completed with some state attorneys general challenging the
agreement. Together the combined business is now one of the largest networking vendors in the world competing head-on with Cisco across
campus data center and service provider networks.
Aruba's acquisitions show how it grew from Wi-Fi into a full edgetocloud networking platform. From 2007 to 2013,
it added wireless security, multi- vendor management, outdoor mesh, network access control, and indoor location.
From 2015 to 2020 as part of HPE, it added analytics, user behavior
analytics, network sensors, and SDWAN with Silver Peak. And from 2023, private
5G security service edge, and finally, Juniper Networks, the deal that created HPE networking.
Aruba's revenue grew from tens of millions of dollars in its early years to several hundred million as an
independent company. Inside HPE, the networking business at Anchored has grown into a run rate of more than 11
billion a year. Its lasting contributions include controller-based Wi-Fi, identity- based networking, clear
pass, Aruba central, CX switching, and edge connect SDWAN. It competes with Cisco, Extreme Networks, Fortnet,
Ubiquiti, and Huaway in campus networks and with Cisco and Arista in the data center. From a Sunale startup betting on
wireless to the heart of a combined HPE and Juniper networking business, Aruba helped make mobility the default way we
connect at work. Thanks for watching this episode of networking landscape. Next, we'll look at F5.

v7fV1eZtIYc.title: Zscaler EP11
tx: For decades, corporate security meant building a wall around the network and sending every user's traffic back
through it. In 2007, a serial entrepreneur bet that the wall itself would disappear and that security should
move into the cloud between users and the applications they use. This is the story of Zcaler, a founder who had
already sold four security companies. A cloud built from scratch to inspect internet traffic. The move from VPNs to
zero trust, the zero trust exchange, and the push into security operations and AI will follow six chapters. The founder, a
security cloud, zero trust private access, the IPO and the pandemic, the zero trust exchange, and Zcaler in the AI era.
J Chow Dri grew up in a small village in the Himalayan foothills of northern India in a home without electricity or running water for much of his childhood.
He came to the United States for graduate studies at the University of Cincinnati. After working at large technology companies including IBM, he
became a serial entrepreneur in security. Each company taught him something about where security was heading. from the server to email to
wireless and finally to the network itself dissolving as users and applications left the office. His first
company secure it was sold to very sign in 1998.
Core harbor followed. Cipher trust an email security company was sold to secure computing in 2006 and air defense
a wireless security company was sold to Motorola in 2008. In 2007, Chowodri
founded Zcaler with K. Kai Lash, investing much of his own money to build it. The name comes from the idea of the
zenith of scalability. For its first years, Zscaler was largely self-funded and kept a low profile while its
engineers built a global cloud infrastructure, one data center at a time.
Zcaler's idea was a sharp break from the traditional model. In the old Castellin mode approach, branch offices and remote
users sent their traffic back to a central data center over MLS or VPN where it passed through a stack of
firewalls and web proxies before reaching the internet. Zcaler instead put the security stack in its own cloud.
Users connect to the nearest Zscaler data center where their traffic is inspected and then go straight to the internet or the SAS application without
being backhauled through the corporate network. As applications moved to the cloud, especially Microsoft 365,
this approach removed a major bottleneck and reduced the need for security appliances in every branch. It also
meant the same policy applied wherever a user worked in the office, at home or on the road because the security followed the user rather than the network.
Zcaler launched its cloud security platform in 2008. The service that grew from it Zcaler internet access or ZIA is a cloud-d delivered secure web gateway.
ZIA works as a proxy. It inspects web traffic, including encrypted traffic, filters URLs, blocks malware, sandboxes
suspicious files, and applies data loss prevention, all from the cloud with no hardware at the customer's site. The
architecture was built from scratch for multi-tenency and scale rather than by putting virtual appliances in a data center, a difference Chowri has
emphasized for years. Inspecting encrypted traffic at scale was critical because by the late 2010s, most web
traffic used TLS and attackers were hiding malware inside it. For years, Zcaler was rated a leader in Gartner's
evaluations of secure web gateways and large enterprises gradually replaced their on premises web proxies with ZIA.
The next step was private applications.
The ones running in a company's own data centers or clouds. Traditionally, remote users reach those applications through a
VPN which put them on the corporate network where malware or attackers could move freely. Zcaler private access or
ZPA launched in the mid2010s connects users directly to individual applications never to the network. Small
software connectors next to the applications make outbound connections to the Zscaler cloud. So the applications are invisible to the
internet. This became one of the first widely deployed examples of zero trust network access or ZTNA.
Every request is checked against the user's identity, the devices posture and policy before any connection is made.
Zcaler argued that this made the attack surface disappear. If applications are not exposed to the internet, attackers
cannot find them. And if users are never placed on the network, they cannot move laterally.
In March 2018, Zcaler went public on NASDAQ under the ticker ZS, raising $192
million. Its shares roughly doubled on the first day of trading. In 2020, the COVID pandemic sent much of the world's
workforce home overnight. Companies whose VPN concentrators were overwhelmed turned to ZP and ZIA and Zcaler's growth
accelerated. The pandemic turned zero trust from a niche idea into a board level priority and many organizations
began retiring VPNs altogether. In December 2021, Zscaler joined the NASDAQ
100 index. The company also built a large ecosystem of partners integrating with identity providers such as Octa and
Microsoft and point security vendors such as Crowdstrike and SDWAN vendors.
Zcaler now calls its platform the zero trust exchange, the world's largest inline cloud security platform by its
own description. In October 2024, Zscaler said its cloud was processing more than 500 billion transactions a day
across more than 160 data centers and blocking more than 150 million threats daily. That scale gives Zscaler a large
view of internet threats, which its threat labs research team uses to publish regular reports on ransomware,
fishing, and encrypted attacks. The zero trust exchange extends zero trust to branches, factories, cloud workloads,
and IoT devices, not just users, and adds digital experience monitoring, data protection, and deception technology. In
Gartner's 2026 magic quadrant for sassy platforms, Zcaler entered the leaders quadrant for the first time alongside
Netscope, Kado Networks, and Palo Alto Networks. and it was also named a leader for security service edge.
To broaden the platform, Zscaler has made a steady series of acquisitions. In 2020, it bought Cloud Needy for cloud
security posture and edge wise for workload segmentation. In 2021, it added Trust Dome and Smokescreen, a deception
technology company. In 2024, it acquired Avalor for about $310 million, whose
data fabric for security became the basis for Zscaler's risk management and security operations products and Air Gap
networks for segmentation inside branches and campuses. In 2025, it announced the acquisition of Red Canary,
a managed detection and response company, moving Zcaler into security operations. And in 2026, it announced
the purchase of Square X for browser security. Red Canary added about 141 million of annual recurring revenue in
fiscal 2026 and gave Zscaler a team of security analysts and an established detection and response service.
Zcaler now describes itself as the cyber security platform for the AI era. Its focus areas are zero trust, sassy,
agentic security operations, data security, and security for AI, protecting how employees use AI
applications, and how AI agents access data and systems. It offers controls to see which AI applications employees use,
to stop sensitive data from being pasted into them, and to apply guardrails to prompts and responses. Its argument is
that the same zero trust principles apply to AI agents as to people. Every agent should be authenticated given only
the access it needs and have its traffic inspected. Zcaler also uses the huge volume of data passing through its cloud
to train its own AI models for threat detection, data classification, and risk scoring.
Zcalers fiscal year 2026 ended in July.
Revenue reached $3.35 billion, up 25% including Red Canary. Annual recurring
revenue reached $3.77 billion also up 25% with $246 million of net new ARR in
the fourth quarter alone. For fiscal 2027, Zscaler guided to revenue of about
3.91 to $3.94 billion, growth of roughly 17%. Growth is slowing from the very
high rates of earlier years, but Zscala remains one of the largest pure cloud security companies with gross margins of
about 80%. Jay Chowri still leads the company he founded nearly two decades ago as chairman and chief executive.
Zcaler's acquisitions show how its platform has expanded beyond the web gateway. From 2018 to 20121, it added AI
and machine learning, browser isolation, cloud security, workload segmentation and deception technology. From 2022 to
2024, it moved into security workflow automation, SAS security, a data fabric
for security operations and segmentation inside the network. And from 2025, Red Canary and Square X took it into managed
detection and response and browser security.
In eight years as a public company, Zscaler's annual revenue grew from about $190 million to more than three $3
billion. Its lasting products include Zscaler Internet Access, Zcaler Private Access, the Zero Trust Exchange, and a
growing set of services for data protection, security operations, and AI security. It competes with Paulo, Alto
Networks, Netscope, Cisco, Cloudflare, and Fortnet in sassy and security service edge and with Crowd Strike and
others in security operations. From a bet that the network perimeter would disappear to the security cloud for the
AI era, Zcaler helped turn zero trust from a concept into an architecture used by many of the world's largest
companies. Thanks for watching this episode of Networking Landscape. That completes our security season.

a_k8s2OBnrQ.title: Check Point EP10
tx: In 1993, three young Israelis set out to protect companies connecting to the internet. Their product Firewall 1
introduced a technique called stateful inspection and it became the foundation of the modern firewall. Their company
Checkpoint Software Technologies has been a leader in network security ever since. This is the story of Checkpoint,
the invention of stateful inspection, the partnerships with Sun and Nokia, a failed attempt to buy SourceFire, the
move to threat prevention and the Infinity platform, and a new chief executive for the AI era. We'll follow
six chapters, the founding and firewall one, market leadership and the IPO, the Nokia years, threat prevention, cloud
and sassy, and checkpoint under new leadership.
Gilshwed started working as a system administrator at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem while still a teenager.
During his military service, reportedly in the intelligence unit 8,200, he worked on secure computer networks.
After the army, Shwed joined a company called Optro Tech where he met Marius Knocked. Together with Schlommo Kramer,
who had served with Shwed in the military, they began developing a firewall in 1993. All three were in their early 20s.
Checkpoint was founded in July 1993 in Ramat Gone, Israel. The founders reportedly spent about a year writing the software in a relative's apartment.
In 1994, Firewall 1 debuted at the Networld Plus Interop Show in Las Vegas and won the best of show award. Early
funding came from BRM, an Israeli technology group, and the timing was perfect. Businesses were just starting
to connect their internal networks to the public internet, and they needed a way to keep intruders out.
The key innovation was stateful inspection, which SHW developed and patented. Early firewalls used simple
packet filters, examining each packet on its own against a list of rules. They could not tell whether a packet belonged
to a legitimate conversation, so attackers could slip packets past them.
A stateful firewall keeps a table of active connections. When a user inside the network opens a session, the
firewall records it and only allows return traffic that matches that session. Everything else is dropped.
This gave much stronger security without the heavy overhead of application proxies which were the other main approach at the time. Stateful
inspection remains at the core of nearly every firewall today including next generation firewalls. Firewall 1 also
introduced a graphical policy editor which made firewall rules much easier to manage than the command lines used by most competitors.
Checkpoint grew rapidly through partnerships. In 1994, Sun Micro Systemystems signed an OEM agreement to
resell Firewall 1 and HP followed about a year later. In June 1996, Checkpoint
went public on NASDAQ under the ticker CHKP.
Soon after, it launched VPN, adding encrypted virtual private networks to its firewall. In 1997,
it created Opsac, the open platform for security, an alliance that let hundreds of other vendors integrate their
products with Checkpoints management. By the late 1990s, Checkpoint was widely regarded as the market leader in
firewalls, and its software ran on servers and appliances from many hardware partners. In 1998, it began a
long partnership with Nokia, whose IP series appliances were among the most popular platforms for running Checkpoint
software. Unlike many rivals, Checkpoint remained mainly a software company, selling through partners and resellers
and earning high margins on licenses and subscriptions.
The three founders went in different directions. Gilshwed served as chief executive for more than three decades,
one of the longest tenurs of any technology company founder. Marius Knock stayed with Checkpoint for many years
and later became a major investor in Israeli health technology startups.
Schlommo Kramer left to co-founder, a data and application security company in 2002 and later Kado Networks in 2015.
one of the pioneers of Sassy, which we met in our first episode.
In the 2000s, Checkpoint expanded beyond the network firewall. In 2004, it bought Zone Labs, maker of the popular Zone
Alarm personal firewall, moving into endpoint security. In 2005, it agreed to buy SourceFire, creator of the Snort
intrusion detection engine, for about $225 million. But the deal faced national security scrutiny in the United
States and Checkpoint abandoned it in 2006.
Sourcefire was later bought by Cisco. In 2009, Checkpoint acquired Nokia's network security appliance business,
taking control of the hardware platforms that ran much of its software. That same year, it introduced its software blade
architecture, letting customers turn on security functions as modules. The Nokia deal ended a successful partnership, but
it also meant Checkpoint now competed directly as an appliance vendor against fast growing rivals like Fortnet and soon Paulo Alto Networks.
As attacks grew more sophisticated, Checkpoint shifted its message from detection to prevention. In 2012, it
launched Threat Cloud, a collaborative intelligence network that shares information about new threats among checkpoint gateways and endpoints
worldwide. In 2015, it introduced Sand Blast with thread emulation, which runs suspicious files in a sandbox, and
thread extraction, which removes risky content from documents before they reach users. Checkpoints research team became
known for discovering major vulnerabilities and malware campaigns and its threat reports became a regular
reference for the industry. In 2018, Checkpoint launched its Infinity architecture, a unified platform
covering networks, cloud, mobile, and endpoints with a single management system. It described this as fifth
generation cyber security against largecale multi-vector attacks.
Checkpoint then moved into cloud security and secure access. In 2018, it bought Dome 9, a cloud security posture
management company, which became the core of CloudGuard. In 2021, it acquired Avaan, which protects cloud email and
collaboration tools such as Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace. In 2023, it
bought Perimeter 81, an Israeli sassy company to build Harmony Sassy and Atmosc for SAS security. In 2024, it
added Cyber int for external risk management. These acquisitions turned Checkpoint from a firewall vendor into a
broader platform company, though still with network security at its core.
Today, Checkpoint organizes its products around the Infiniti platform. Quantum covers its network firewalls from small
business appliances to hypers scale data center systems along with remote access VPN. Cloudg guard secures public cloud
networks and applications. And harmony protects users and devices with email security, endpoint protection, browser
security and sassy. Underneath Threat Cloud AI provides threat intelligence and prevention engines while Infiniti
external risk management watches for threats outside the corporate network.
In December 2024, Checkpoint announced a leadership change. Gil Shwed became executive chairman and Nadav Zafrier
became chief executive. Zafrier is a former commander of unit 8,200 and co-founder of team 8, a venture
group that builds cyber security companies. Under Zafrier, Checkpoint launched an AI first strategy. In 2025,
it bought Very T for threat exposure management and Lira an AI security company that protects AI applications
and agents. In 2026, it acquired Sai Ata and Cyclops, extending its work on
securing AI agents and exposure management. Zafrier's message was that AI changes both sides of security.
Attackers use AI to move faster while defenders need AI to keep up and to protect the AI systems that companies are now deploying.
Checkpoint is famously profitable with some of the highest operating margins in the software industry. In 2025, revenue
grew 6% to $2.73 billion and adjusted earnings per share grew about 30%. For
2026, Checkpoint guided to revenue of $2.83 to $2.95 billion.
In the first quarter of 2026, revenue grew 5% to $668 million as subscription
revenue grew while appliance sales faced near-term headwinds. Growth has been slower than Apollo Alto Networks or
Fortnet. Checkpoint's challenge under its new leadership is to turn its huge installed base and AI investments into
faster growth. It also keeps returning large amounts of cash to shareholders, buying back hundreds of millions of dollars of its own shares every quarter.
Checkpoint has made relatively few acquisitions for a company of its age, but they mark each step in its
evolution. From 2004 to 2015, it added endpoint security with Zone Labs, the
Nokia appliance business, and threat prevention with Hyperwise. From 2018 to 2024, it moved into the cloud, email,
Sassy, SAS security, and external risk management. And since 2025, it has focused on exposure management and the security of AI.
Over three decades, Checkpoint's revenue grew steadily, past $2.5 billion, while remaining one of the most profitable
companies in software. Its lasting contributions include stateful inspection and firewall 1, VPN 1, the
opsec alliance, threat cloud and the infinity platform with quantum cloudguard and harmony. It competes with
Paulo Alto networks and fortnet in firewalls with Zscaler, Netscope and Kado networks in Sassy and with many
others across email cloud and endpoint security. From a firewall written in an apartment in 1993 to an AI first
security platform, Checkpoint helped invent the industry that the rest of this season describes. Thanks for watching this episode of Networking Landscape.

xt5ugoObYyE.title: Fortinet EP09
tx: Most security companies are software companies. Fortnet took a different path. From the beginning, it designed its own chips so its firewalls could do
more work faster and at lower cost. That bet helped it become by its own count the vendor that ships the most network
firewalls in the world. This is the story of Fortnet. Two brothers, an earlier startup that Juniper bought for
$4 billion. The 40gate custom security processors, the security fabric SDWAN built into every firewall, and the push
into Sassy and security operations will follow six chapters. Kenshay before Fortnet, the founding and the 40 gate,
custom silicon, the IPO and growth, the security fabric and SDWAN, and Fortnet today.
Ken Shay grew up in China, studied atQing HWA University, and came to the United States for graduate school at
Stanford. His brother, Michael Shay, followed a similar path into engineering and would later become his co-founder.
Both believed that security performance would ultimately depend on hardware as well as software. In 1993, he founded
his first network security company, Systems Integration Solutions, which built one of the early firewalls. In
1996, working in his garage in Palo Alto, Shy built one of the first firewall and VPN appliances based on a
custom chip, an Isik with Yan Ka and Fun Dong. He co-founded Netcreen Technologies and became its chief
executive. Netcreen's ASICbased firewalls were fast and successful. Its netscreen 1000 was described as the
first gigabit speed firewall from a firewall maker. In 2004, Juniper Networks bought Netcreen for about $4
billion. But Shy had already left. In 2000, convinced that firewalls alone were not enough, he started again. That
history ties Fortnet directly to Juniper. Netcreen's firewalls became Juniper's security business while its
founder built one of Juniper's strongest competitors.
In 2000, Ken Shay and his brother Michael founded a company first called Obligation, then AppScure, and finally
Fortnet. Ken became chief executive, and Michael became president and chief technology officer. Their idea was to
combine many security functions into one appliance. Firewall, VPN, antivirus, intrusion prevention, and web filtering.
The industry later called this unified threat management or UTM. In May 2002, Fortnet launched its first 40 gate
appliances running its own operating system, 40 OS. Antivirus and anti-PAM products followed. Unified threat
management appealed especially to small and midsized businesses which could not afford separate appliances and specialists for every security function.
In 2005, Fortnet created 40 guard labs, its threat research team, which delivers updated signatures and threat
intelligence to every 40 gate as a subscription service. That combination, hardware sold once, plus security
subscriptions renewed every year, became Fortnet's business model, and services now make up the majority of its revenue.
Fortnet's defining technical choice was to keep designing its own chips, as Shy had done at Netcreen. A firewall running
only on generalpurpose processors must do everything in software, from routing packets to scanning content for threats.
As more security features are switched on, performance can drop sharply.
Fortnite's 40 gates use custom security processors. Network processors or NPS accelerate firewall and VPN traffic.
Content processors or CPS accelerate tasks like encryption and thread inspection. And system on a chip designs
such as the SP5 launched in 2021 combine these functions for smaller firewalls.
Later generations such as the NP7 added support for very large numbers of encrypted connections and for protecting
against denial of service attacks in hardware. The result, Fortnet argues, is higher performance, lower power, and a
lower price for the same level of protection. Competitors dispute some of these claims, but custom silicon has been central to Fortnet's ability to
sell in high volumes. From small branch offices to large data centers, Fortnet also uses its chips for other jobs,
including hypers scale firewalls for service providers, which handle huge numbers of sessions for mobile and broadband networks.
Fortnite grew through a large global network of channel partners, focusing first on small and midsized businesses,
then moving steadily up into large enterprises and service providers. The company turned profitable in 2008, and
in November 2009, it went public on NASDAQ under the ticker FTNT, raising
$156 million. In 2010, annual revenue reached $324 million. The IPO came in
the middle of the financial crisis, making Fortnet one of the few technology companies to go public that year. In
2014, Fortnet launched its network security expert certification program, training hundreds of thousands of
engineers on its products. That same year, it co-founded the cyber threat alliance with its rival Paulo Alto
Networks. Fortnet also expanded by acquisition, buying Maru Networks for Wi-Fi in 2015 and Excel Ops in 2016, whose security analytics became 40 seam.
In 2016, Fortnet introduced the security fabric, an architecture connecting its products so they could share information
and respond together. The 40 gate became the center. 40 switches and 40 AP access points could be managed directly from
it, turning the firewall into a controller for the whole branch or campus network. Further acquisitions filled gaps in the fabric. Bradford
Networks in 2018 added network access control, now 40 Knack. N silo in 2019
added endpoint detection and response, now 40 EDR. and cyerspon added security
orchestration now 40 sore 40 OS ties the fabric together with a single operating system and a single management console
40 manager for thousands of devices in 2017 also created fortnet federal a
subsidiary focused on US government customers next big win came from SDWAN as branch
offices moved from expens expensive MLS circuits to broadband. They needed SDWAN and they still needed a firewall.
Fortnet built SDWAN directly into 40 OS.
So every 40 gate could act as both with no additional license for SDWAN. For customers, that meant one less box in
every branch and one less vendor to manage. A strong argument for retailers and banks operating thousands of
locations. This secure SDWAN approach became one of the most widely deployed in the market, especially with
retailers, banks, and other companies with thousands of branches. In July 2020, Fortnet added multicloud SDWAN.
Fortnet's pitch was convergence networking and security in a single operating system and a single box rather
than separate products from separate vendors.
As users and applications moved to the cloud, Fortnet extended the same idea into Sassy. In 2020, it bought APAC
Networks, a cloud security startup which helped form 40 Sassy, its cloud-d delivered security service. Fortinet
describes its approach as unified Sassy, combining 40 Sassy with its SDWAN and 40 OS everywhere. In Gartner's 2026 magic
quadrant for sassy platforms, Fortnet moved from the leaders quadrant to challengers after only one year as a
leader, but customer adoption kept growing. In the second quarter of 2026, 40 sassy billings more than doubled. In
2024, Fortnet bought Lace Work for cloud security and next DLP for data loss prevention, expanding its platform into cloud workloads and data protection.
Fortnet also added foria, generative AI assistants that help analysts investigate incidents and configure the platform in plain language.
Today, the Fortnet security fabric spans more than 50 products. At its core are 40 gate firewalls and 40 OS from small
branch models to large data center and service provider systems plus virtual and cloud versions. Around them sit
secure networking products 40 switch, 40 and 40 knack and the sassy portfolio with 40 sassy, SDWAN and zero trust
access. And on the operations side, 40 seam, 40 sore, 40 ed, and 40 analyzer.
Increasingly driven by AI alongside a growing business in operational technology security for factories, utilities, and critical infrastructure.
Fortnet entered 2026 with a strong firewall refresh cycle. In the third quarter of 2026, revenue grew 20% to
$2.08 08 billion. Product revenue, mostly 40gate hardware, rose 37% and billings grew 29% to 2 $34 billion.
Fortnet raised its fullear 2026 outlook to revenue of about 8.1 to $8.2 billion,
roughly 20% growth. Services billings, security operations, and operational technology security all grew strongly
too. and Fortnet's operating margins remained among the highest in the industry. Ken and Michael Shyier still
lead the company they founded more than a quarter of a century later. Few founders of a company of this size are still running it.
Fortnet has grown mainly through its own engineering, but acquisitions filled important gaps. From 2013 to 2016, it
added application delivery, Wi-Fi, and security analytics. From 2018 to 20121,
it bought companies for network access control, insider threat detection, endpoint detection and response,
orchestration, and cloud security. And from 2024, it added cloud security with lace work, data loss prevention, and more.
Fortnet's revenue grew from about $324 million in 2010 to more than $8 billion expected in 2026.
Its business model, custom hardware plus recurring security services, has delivered consistent growth and strong
profits through two decades and several technology shifts. Its lasting products include 40 gate and 40 OS, its custom
security processors, the security fabric, secure SDWAN, 40 sassy and 40 guard labs thread intelligence. It
competes with Palpo Alto networks and checkpoint in firewalls with Cisco and HPE in SDWAN and networking and with Zscaler Netscope and others in Sassy.
From a garagebuilt ISIC firewall in 1996 to a security and networking platform used by hundreds of thousands of
customers, Fortnet shows how custom silicon can still be a competitive weapon. Thanks for watching this episode of Networking Landscape.

eM7ub0oZZw0.title: Palo Alto Networks EP08
tx: In 2005, a former checkpoint engineer decided that the firewall, the product he had helped create, was obsolete.
Firewalls looked at ports and IP addresses, but the internet had moved to applications that ignored them. His answer became the next generation
firewall, and the company he founded, Paulo Alto Networks, grew into the largest pureplay cyber security company
in the world. This is the story of Paulo Alto Networks. App ID and the next generation firewall. The move into cloud
security and security operations. An aggressive acquisition strategy under Nash Aurora. The idea of platformization
and the multi-billion dollar bets on identity and observability will follow six chapters. The founding, the next
generation firewall, growth and the IPO, beyond the firewall, the Aurora era and platformization, and the AI era with Cyber Arc.
Near Zuk served in the Israeli military's elite technology unit, Unit 8,200, then joined Checkpoint, where he became
one of the key developers of the company's firewall. He later co-founded One Secure, an intrusion prevention company acquired by Netscreen, where he
became chief technology officer. By 2005, Zuk believed the stateful firewall had reached its limits. Applications
such as instant messaging, file sharing, and web-based services used any open port, often port 80, and could be
encrypted. A firewall that only saw ports and addresses was effectively blind. Zuk's idea was to rebuild the
firewall around three questions. Which application is this? Which user is behind it? And what content is it
carrying? Seuia Capital gave Zuk office space to develop the idea. Paulo Alto Networks was founded on March 1, 2005 by
Zuk and Rajie Batra. And in January 2006, Sequoia and Greylock funded the
company. On June 25, 2007, Paulo Alto Networks unveiled its first product, the
P of 4000 series, which it called a next generation firewall. The P of 4000 was a purpose-built appliance with dedicated
processing for networking, security, and management so that inspecting applications would not slow the network down.
So, what made it next generation? A traditional firewall decides what to allow based on ports and IP addresses.
If port 443 is open, almost anything can pass through it. Paulo Alto's firewall classified traffic by application using
a technology called app ID, no matter which port, protocol, or encryption the application used. User ID tied traffic
to individual users and groups rather than IP addresses. and content ID scanned the traffic for threats,
malware, and sensitive data. All of this happened in a single pass through the traffic on hardware designed for it with
one policy that described which users could use which applications. Gartner adopted the term next generation
firewall and every major firewall vendor eventually followed Paulo Alto's lead.
It also changed how security teams wrote policy. Instead of thousands of port-based rules, administrators could
write rules in business terms such as allowing the marketing team to use social media, but blocking file transfers.
Paulo Alto Networks grew rapidly, taking firewall share from Checkpoint, Cisco, and Juniper. In 2011, Mark Mclofflin,
formerly a very sign, became chief executive, while Zuk remained chief technology officer. Its success brought
legal battles too. Juniper sued Paulo Alto over patents in 2011 and the companies settled in 2014 with Paulo
Alto agreeing to pay $175 million. In 2011, it also launched Wildfire, a
cloud-based sandbox that detonated suspicious files to detect previously unknown malware, an early example of
security delivered from the cloud. On July 20, 2012, Paulo Alto Networks went public on the New York Stock Exchange,
raising $260 million. In its fiscal year 2012, revenue was about $400 million. In
2014, Paulo Alto Networks and Fortnet, two fierce rivals, co-founded the Cyber Threat Alliance to share threat
intelligence across the security industry.
To keep growing, Palo Alto Networks expanded beyond the firewall. In 2014, it bought Sai Vera, an Israeli endpoint
security startup for about $200 million, which became its traps and point protection product. As companies moved
to the cloud, it launched virtual and container firewalls, the VM series and later the CN series, and bought evident
IO and Redlock in 2018 to secure public cloud environments, the foundation of Prisma cloud. Its firewalls also moved
into the public clouds themselves, available in the marketplaces of AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud, so
customers could apply the same policies everywhere. In 2017, it acquired Light Cyber for behavioral analytics and began
collecting data from firewalls and endpoints into a central data lake, setting the stage for its security operations business.
In June 2018, Nikesh Aurora became chairman and chief executive. He had been a senior executive at Google and
president of SoftBank and he had no background in cyber security. Aurora accelerated acquisitions dramatically.
In 2019 alone, Paulo Alto bought Demyista for security automation, Twist Lock for container security, Pure Sec
for serverless security, Zingbox for IoT security, and Aporeto for micro segmentation. Critics questioned whether
so many products could be integrated, but Aurora argued that customers wanted fewer, larger security vendors and that
Paulo Alto had to be one of them. In 2020, it bought Cloud Genics for about $420 million, adding SDWAN and expanse
for about $1.25 billion for attack surface management. Aurora reorganized the company around three platforms.
Strata for network security, Prisma for cloud and secure access and Cordex for security operations launched in 2019.
Each platform has its own family of products. Strada covers the next generation firewalls in hardware,
virtual, container, and cloudnative forms managed through Strata Cloud Manager. Prisma Sassy combines Prisma
Access, a cloud-d delivered security service with Prisma SDWAN. It was later extended with an enterprise browser from
the 20123 acquisition of Talon. Cordex includes XDR for endpoint detection and
response. Exor for automation, expanse for attack surface management, and XIAM,
an AIdriven security operations platform designed to replace the traditional seam. And Cordexcloud combines cloud security with security operations.
Precision AI, Palo Alto's umbrella name for its AI and machine learning, runs across all three platforms, analyzing
huge volumes of telemetry from firewalls, endpoints, and clouds.
In February 2024, Paulo Alto announced a strategy it called platformization, persuading customers to consolidate many
security tools onto its platforms, even offering some products free for a period to speed up the switch. Investors were
initially alarmed and the stock fell sharply the next day, but the strategy became central to Paulo Alto's growth
and its competitors adopted similar platform pitches. In practice, platformization meant bundling larger
multi-year deals spanning network security, cloud security, and security operations with financial incentives to
retire competitors tools. To accelerate XIAM, Paulo Alto agreed in 2024 to buy
IBM's Q Radar software as a service business and to migrate Q Radar customers to its own platform. In secure
access, Prisma Sassy became one of the market leaders in Gartner's 2026 Magic Quadrant for sassy platforms. Paulo Alto
remained a leader, though it slipped from first to third, partly because of its reportedly high pricing. Its firewalls remained a franchise, too.
Paulo Alto continued to launch new hardware generations, and its software firewalls protected traffic inside clouds and data centers.
Paulo Alto's biggest bets came in 2025.
In July 2025, it agreed to buy Cyber Ark, the leader in privileged access and identity security, for about $25 billion, by far its largest acquisition.
The deal was completed in February 2026, adding identity to network security, cloud security, and security operations.
It also bought Kronosphere, an observability company, for $3.35 billion
completed in January 2026, bringing large-scale telemetry and monitoring data into its platforms. And it moved
quickly into AI security with protect AI in 2025, Koi Security and Console in 2026, and an agreement to buy port key.
The thesis is that AI agents are a new class of identity and they will need to be secured like people. With Cyber Arc,
Paulo Alto can now combine network security, identity, and security operations in a single platform, a
combination no other security company matches at its scale.
Paulo Alto's fiscal year 2026 ended in July. Revenue reached 11.48 48 billion,
up from 9.22 billion the year before. In the fourth quarter, revenue grew 34% to 341 billion.
Next Generation Security annual recurring revenue, which tracks its newer platforms, reached $9.1 billion,
up 63%, and the company added nearly $1 billion of it in a single quarter.
Remaining performance obligations reached 21 $2 billion for fiscal 2027.
Paulo Alto guided to revenue of about 14.1 to 14.2 billion growth of about 23
to 24%. Profitability also remained strong with an adjusted free cash flow
margin of about 38% in fiscal 2026 even as the company absorbed the costs of its largest acquisitions.
Few security companies have bought as many businesses as Paulo Alto Networks.
From 2014 to 2018 early deals like Saiver, Light Cyber, Evident.io O and
Redlock took it into endpoints and the cloud. From 2019 to 2023 under Aurora
came a rapid series of acquisitions from Demyist and Twist Lock to Expanse, Cloud Genics, Talon, and DIG. And from 2025, a
new wave of much larger deals, Cyber Arc, Chronosphere, and a string of AI security companies.
In 14 years as a public company, Paulo Alto's annual revenue grew from about $400 million to nearly 11 5 billion. Its
lasting products include App ID and the next generation firewall, Prisma Access and Prisma Sassy, Prisma Cloud, Cordex
XDR and XSAM, and now Cyber Arcs identity security. It competes with Fortnet and Checkpoint in firewalls,
with Zscaler, Netscope and Cisco in Sassy, with Crowd Strike and Microsoft in endpoint security and security
operations, and with many others from one engineer's insight that firewalls should understand applications to a
platform for securing networks, clouds, identities, and AI agents, Paulo Alto Networks has set the direction of the
security industry for nearly two decades. Thanks for watching this episode of Networking Landscape.

Ubq2aRllX3k.title: Broadcom History EP07
tx: Open up a switch from Arista, a white box running Sonic or many models from Cisco and Juniper, and there is a good
chance you will find the same company's chip inside. That company is Broadcom.
This is the story of how two very different companies, a UCL, a startup, and a spin-off of Huelet Packard's chip
division, came together to become the most important supplier of networking silicon in the world and one of the most
valuable companies on Earth. will follow six chapters, two origins, the merchant silicon revolution, Jericho and Deep
Buffers, Avago's takeover and Hawkton's acquisition machine, VMware and Software, and the AI era of custom accelerators and 100 terab switches.
The first origin is Broadcom Corporation. It was founded in August 1991 by Henry Samuelli, a UCL
engineering professor and Henry Nicholas, one of his students, to build chips for broadband communication.
Broadcom went public on NASDAQ in 1998 and grew into a leader in chips for cable modems, set top boxes, DSL,
Ethernet, and later Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, which ended up in billions of smartphones. The second origin goes back
much further to 1961 when Huelet Packard set up a semiconductor division called
HP Associates. In 1999, it moved to the HP spin-off Agyant Technologies. In
2005, private equity firms KKR and Silverlake bought Agyant's chip business for $2.6 billion and named it Avago
Technologies. In 2006, Hawkton became chief executive and in August 2009, Avago went public on NASDAQ.
Broadcom Corporation entered the switch chip business in January 1999 when it bought Maverick Networks, a startup
designing chips for multi-layer network switches for about $14 million. that became the Strata Switch and Strata XGS
families, single chips that could do the switching work of an entire line card.
Broadcom also sold Ethernet physical layer chips and network adapters, putting it inside a huge share of the
world's Ethernet ports. In 2011, Broadcom bought Net Logic micro systemystems for $3.7 billion, adding
knowledgebased processors used for fast route lookups and multi-core network processors. Broadcom's switch chips
started in enterprise and lowcost data center switches. But a much bigger opportunity was about to open up.
Traditionally, network vendors designed their own chips, wrote their own software, and built their own boxes, all
tightly integrated. Broadcom offered another model, merchant silicon. One chip design sold to many vendors who
could focus on software and system design instead of building custom chips for every product. Arista was built on
this model from the start. Over time, Cisco, Juniper, HPE, Dell, and many others used Broadcom chips in some of
their switches, and cloud providers bought white box switches from manufacturers in Taiwan and China running open software such as Sonic.
Merchant silicon also changed the economics. A single Broadcom chip generation could ship in switches from
dozens of brands, spreading the enormous cost of chip design across the whole industry. This disagregation transformed
data center networking. Hardware became a fastmoving commodity and Broadcom became the common platform underneath much of the industry.
Broadcom Strata XGS line split into families for different jobs. Trident chips targeted enterprise and data center switches with rich features.
Trident Roman 2 in 2012 delivered 1.28 28 terabs per second and powered a generation of 10 and 40 Gbit data center
switches. In 2014, Broadcom introduced Tomahawk built for the cloud with 3.2
tabs per second and support for 25, 50, and 100 GB Ethernet. Later, Trident generations added programmability so features could be updated in software.
While Tomahawk focused on raw bandwidth and power efficiency for the largest cloud networks. From there, Tomahawk
roughly doubled in capacity every 2 years or so. 6.4 tabs, then 12.8, 25.6, and 51.2 tabs with Tomahawk 5 in 2022.
Each generation set the pace for the whole data center switching industry.
Not every network wants the fastest possible chip. Routers and large modular switches need deep packet buffers and
huge forwarding tables. In December 2009, Broadcom bought Dune Networks, an Israeli chip startup for $178 million.
Its technology became the Strata DNx family with AAD and later Jericho launched in 2015. Jericho chips use
external memory to hold gigabytes of packet buffers and millions of routes and they can be linked through fabric chips into large modular systems. They
became the basis for many spine switches and routers built on merchant silicon including platforms from Arista and
Cisco. Later generations added Jericho 3 AI for AI clusters and in August 2025
Jericho 4 which uses high bandwidth memory for buffering and can connect AI data centers more than 100 km apart.
Meanwhile, Hawkton was turning Avago into an acquisition machine. His strategy was to buy companies with
leading technology franchises, cut costs sharply, sell or close businesses that were not market leaders, and invest
heavily in the ones that were. On May 28, 2015, Avago announced its biggest deal yet, the acquisition of Broadcom
Corporation for $ 37 billion in cash and stock. The deal closed on February 1,
2016. The combined company took the Broadcom name and kept the AVgo ticker.
Broadcom's founders Samu Elli and Nicholas had built one of the great communications chip companies and Samu
Ellie joined the new board. True to form, Broadcom sold noncore units such as its internet of things business, sold
to Cyprus for $550 million, and doubled down on networking, broadband, and wireless.
The acquisitions kept coming. In 2014, Avago had bought LSI, a storage
chipmaker, for 6.6 billion and PLX technology, whose PCI Express switches
connect processors inside servers. In 2015, it bought Emullex and in 2017,
Briade, the leader in fiber channel storage networking. Each deal followed a similar playbook. focus on the largest
customers, invest in the most critical products, and cut costs everywhere else.
In November 2017, Broadcom moved its legal home from Singapore to the United States. That same month, it launched an
unsolicited bid for Qualcomm valued at more than $100 billion. In March 2018,
the US government blocked the deal on national security grounds. Broadcom then turned to software. It bought CA
Technologies for $18.9 billion in 2018 and Semantex Enterprise Security Business for 10 $7 billion in 2019.
In May 2022, Broadcom announced its largest acquisition ever, VMware, the leader in server virtualization.
The deal closed on November 22, 2023, valued at about $69 billion.
Broadcom quickly reorganized VMware around VMware Cloud Foundation, moved customers from perpetual licenses to
subscriptions, and cut its product line, a shift that angered many customers, but sharply increased profitability. It also
sold parts of VMware. The end-user computing business went to KKR for $4
billion in 2024 and the VOC cloud SDWAN business went to Arista in 2025.
Infrastructure software is now a major part of Broadcom. In the third quarter of fiscal 2026, it brought in $ 8.75
billion, about 30% of total revenue.
Then came AI and Broadcom's networking business found itself at the center of the largest buildout in data center
history. In June 2025, Broadcom began shipping Tomahawk 6, the first switch
chip with 102.4 terabts per second built for clusters of 100,000 to a million
accelerators with a co-acked optics version. In July 2025, Tomahawk Ultra
targeted scaleup networks inside AI racks with very low latency and Broadcom proposed its scaleup Ethernet framework
as an open alternative to proprietary interconnects like NVLink. Broadcom was also a founding member of the
ultraethernet consortium and argues that open standard Ethernet should connect every part of an AI cluster. In October
2025, it introduced Thor Ultra, an 800 GB AI network card compliant with the Ultra Ethernet specification.
Broadcom now offers chips for every layer of the AI network, scale up, scale out, scale across, and the network card.
Broadcom's other AI business is custom accelerators, which it calls XPS. For about a decade, Broadcom has worked with
Google on its tensor processing units, and it designs custom AI chips for several other large customers, combining
their architectures with Broadcom's chip design, packaging, and high-speed connectivity. Each program is a deep
multi-year partnership. The customer defines the architecture and Broadcom brings the process technology, advanced
packaging, memory interfaces, and the high-speed SDS that move data on and off the chip. In October 2025, Open AI and
Broadcom announced a partnership to develop 10 gawatts of custom AI accelerators and rack systems with deployment starting in the second half
of 2026 and continuing through 2029 connected with Ethernet. Custom accelerators and networking together
make Broadcom the main alternative to Nvidia for companies that want to build their own AI infrastructure.
The results have been extraordinary. In fiscal 2025, Broadcom's revenue reached about $63.9 billion. In the third
quarter of fiscal 2026, revenue was a record $29.6 billion, up 86% and AI
semiconductor revenue was $16.7 billion, up 221%.
For the fourth quarter, Broadcom guided to about $34.8 $8 billion in revenue, including 217 billion from AI chips.
Networking remains a large part of that AI business because every new cluster of custom accelerators or GPS needs
switches, network cards, and optics to connect it. Its market value passed $1 trillion in December 2024 and $2
trillion in April 2026, making Broadcom one of the most valuable companies in the world.
Broadcom is above all a company built by acquisitions. Before 2016, Broadcom Corporation bought Maverick Networks,
Dune Networks, and Net Logic, the foundations of its networking chips.
Avago assembled a semiconductor powerhouse with SCI optics, LSI, PLX, MUX, Broadcom itself, and Briade. Then
came the software era with CA, Semantex, Enterprise Business, and VMware along with sales of businesses it did not want to keep.
Broadcom's switch chips tell their own story from 1.28 terabs per second with Trident Roman 2 in 2012 to 102.4 4
terabs with Tomahawk 6 in 2025, an 80fold increase in 13 years. Its key
networking lines include the Trident and Tomahawk switch chips, the Jericho and Kumron deep buffer chips, Thor network
cards, PCI Express switches, and custom AI accelerators. Broadcom competes with
Nvidia in AI networking and accelerators with Marvel in custom silicon and networking chips and with Cisco's
silicon 1 in switch silicon. From a UCLA startup and an HP chip division to the silicon underneath the AI era, Broadcom
is the company that made merchant networking possible. Thanks for watching this episode of Networking Landscape.

AAGENj62DKk.title: Nokia History EP06
tx: Few technology companies have reinvented themselves as many times as Nokia. It
began as a paper mill in 1,865, became an industrial conglomerate, then the world's largest maker of mobile
phones, and finally one of the world's leading suppliers of network infrastructure. This is the story of Nokia's networks business. From the
first GSM call to Nokia Seammen's networks, the acquisition of Alcatel Lucent and Bell Labs, IP routing and
optical networks, 5G, and today's push into AI and data centers will follow six
chapters. The industrial roots, the birth of mobile, the phone era, Nokia seammen's networks, Alcatel Lucent and Bell Labs, and the AI era.
In 1,865, mining engineer Frederick E. Destham opened a wood pulp mill on the Tamarcausski Rapids in southern Finland.
A few years later, he built a second mill by the Nokian Vera River. And in 1,871, the company took its name from the town
that grew around it, Nokia. In the early 20th century, two other Finnish companies grew up alongside it. The
Finnish rubber works made boots and tires and the Finnish cable works made telephone and power cables. The three
companies became closely linked and in 1967 they merged to form Nokia Corporation, a conglomerate spanning paper, rubber, cables, and electronics.
Over the following decades, the conglomerate made everything from rubber boots and car tires to televisions and personal computers and became one of
Finland's largest companies. The cable business turned out to be the seed of Nokia's future. Its electronics division
began working on computers and telecommunications equipment in the 1960s.
In the 1970s and 1980, Nokia built a telecom business. Its DX200 digital
telephone exchange developed from the late 1970s became a long-lived switching platform
used by operators around the world. In 1981, the Nordic mobile telephone network NMT launched in the Nordic
countries. One of the world's first international cellular networks. Nokia's mobile phone company, Moira, built
phones for it, including the famous Moira Cinnamon of 1987.
Then came GSM, the new European digital mobile standard. On July 1, 1991,
Finland's prime minister, Harry Hall Kerry, made the world's first GSM phone call on a network built by Nokia for the
operator Radio Lineia. Nokia became one of the leading suppliers of GSM network equipment. By the mid '90s, it sold both
the phones and the networks they ran on, an unusual combination that gave it deep insight into mobile technology. In
January 1992, Jorma Ali became chief executive. He decided to focus Nokia
entirely on telecommunications and over the following years sold off its paper, rubber, cable, and consumer electronics businesses.
The bet paid off spectacularly. In 1998, Nokia overtook Motorola to become the world's largest mobile phone maker, a position it held for more than a decade.
Phones like the Nokia 3310, launched in 2000, became cultural icons. At its peak
in 2008, Nokia sold nearly four out of every 10 mobile phones in the world. Its scale was extraordinary. In the early
2000s, Nokia was one of the most valuable brands in the world and accounted for a large share of Finland's exports. But the smartphone era, which
began with Apple's iPhone in 2007 and Google's Android, caught Nokia flatfooted. Its SIMB B and software fell
behind, and in 2011, it switched to Microsoft's Windows phone. In April 2014, Nokia completed the sale of its
devices and services business to Microsoft. What remained was mainly its networks business, its maps business called here, and its patents.
Nokia's networks business had followed a different path. In 2007, Nokia and Seammens combined their network
equipment businesses into a joint venture, Nokia Seammen's Networks, with Nokia owning just over half. The joint
venture struggled with low margins and intense competition from Ericson and from fast growing Chinese suppliers,
especially Huaway. In 2011, it bought most of Motorola's wireless network business under its chief executive Rajie
Suri. It went through a deep restructuring focusing on mobile broadband and services. In 2013, Nokia
bought out Seaman's stake for about €2.2 billion. In 2015, Nokia sold here to a
consortium of German car makers for $2.8 billion.
Nokia was now above all a network infrastructure company, and Siri had become chief executive of the whole group.
On April 15, 2015, Nokia announced its boldest move, an all stock deal to
acquire Alcatel Lucent, valued at 15 €6 billion. Alcatel Lucent itself was the product of two great telecom lineages.
Alcatel grew out of France's CGE, founded in 1,898.
Lucent Technologies was spun off from AT&T in 1996, taking with it the equipment maker Western Electric and the
famous Bell Labs. The two merged in 2006. The acquisition closed in January
2016. It brought Nokia IP routing, optical transport, fixed broadband access, and a large presence in North
America, turning it into an end-to-end network supplier. Nokia also kept a valuable technology licensing business
built on its huge portfolio of mobile patents which still earns well over a billion euros a year. Integration was
difficult and Nokia faced years of pressure on margins. In 2020, Pekka Lundmark succeeded Siri as chief
executive and launched a new strategy built around technology leadership and investment in research.
The acquisition also made Nokia the owner of Bell Labs, one of the most celebrated research laboratories in
history. Bell Labs scientists invented the transistor in 1947, the foundation of all modern
electronics. Claude Shannon published information theory there in 1948, the mathematical basis of digital
communications. The lab also produced the first practical silicon solar cell, early work on the laser, the Unix
operating system, and the C programming language. Its researchers discovered the cosmic microwave background radiation,
evidence for the Big Bang. Bell Labs also developed the concept of the cellular network itself, dividing
territory into cells that reuse radio frequencies, the idea behind every mobile network today. According to
Nokia, work at Bell Labs has been recognized with 10 Nobel prizes. Today, Nokia Bell Labs focuses on 6G, optical
communications, AI for networks, and quantum technologies.
Nokia's IP routing business also came from Alcatel Lucent. In 2003, Alcatel bought a startup called Tmetra, whose router became the 7750 service router.
The 7750 SR and its SRS software became one of the most widely deployed service provider edge routers in the world used
for business VPNs, mobile backhole and broadband. Like Cisco and Juniper, Nokia designs its own routing silicon, the FP
network processors. FP4 in 2017 was among the first to support 400 GB
Ethernet and FP5 in 2022 scaled to 800 GBs with better power efficiency. Its
routers are also used by large cloud and content companies for peering and data center interconnect and its IXR
platforms target data center fabrics including networks for AI workloads. In 2020, Nokia entered data center,
switching with SR Linux, a modern network operating system built on Linux, followed by an event-driven automation
platform. AI and cloud customers are now driving rapid growth. In the third quarter of 2026, Nokia's IP network sales grew 43%.
Optical transport is Nokia's other big bet for the AI era. Alcatel Lucent brought the 1830 photonic service switch
family and Nokia developed its own coherent digital signal processors, the PS series, which set how much data each
wavelength of light can carry. In June 2024, Nokia agreed to buy Infinra, a
pioneer of photonic integrated circuits, for about $2.3 billion. The deal closed
on February 28, 2025, expanding Nokia's optical business, especially with webscale cloud companies in North
America. Nokia also sells pluggable coherent optics, small transceivers that plug directly into routers and switches,
a fast growing segment as data center operators connect their sites over longer distances. AI data centers need
enormous bandwidth between buildings and campuses, and optical networks are how they get it. In the third quarter of
20126, Nokia's optical network sales grew 18%.
Mobile networks remain the largest part of Nokia by headcount and history. Nokia built networks for every generation from
2G GSM through 3G, 4G LTE, and 5G. Its airscale radio and bassband portfolio
powered by its own reef shark chips competes mainly with Ericson and outside the United States and parts of Europe
with Huaway. Nokia has been a strong proponent of open RAN and cloud RAN where radio software runs on
generalpurpose servers and it has won large 5G contracts around the world from Europe to India. The market has been
tough. Operator spending slowed after the first wave of 5G and in December 2023, AT&T chose Ericson for a major
open RAN contract, a significant loss for Nokia in North America. In October 2025, Nvidia invested $1 billion in
Nokia, taking a 2.9% stake to develop AI native radio access networks. Nokia's
radio software is being adapted to run on Nvidia computing platform with trials planned with T-Mobile in the United States.
In April 2025, Justin Hotard became Nokia's chief executive. He came from Intel where he led its data center and
AI business and earlier from Hulet Packard Enterprise. Hotard reorganized Nokia around two main businesses,
network infrastructure and mobile infrastructure, plus a set of portfolio businesses, and put AI and data center customers at the center of its strategy.
The goal is to become a strategic supplier to the companies building AI data centers from hyperscalers to the
new Neoclouds with Nokia's IP and optical networks as the connectivity layer for AI. In 2025, Nokia's net sales
were about 19.9 billion euros. In the third quarter of 2026, net sales grew 9%
at constant currency to 5.2 billion and sales to AI and cloud customers more
than doubled, up 123%. In fixed networks, Nokia remains one of the largest suppliers of fiber broadband
equipment, and it continues to sell private wireless networks to industries such as ports, mines, and factories.
Nokia's modern shape was created by a series of big deals in both directions.
Between 2007 and 2013, it built its networks business with Seammens, then added Motorola's network business and
finally bought out Seammens. Between 2014 and 2016, it sold its phones to Microsoft and here to the car makers and
bought Alcatel Lucent. And since then, it has made smaller technology acquisitions, sold its submarine cable
business to the French state and bought in Finra.
Nokia's revenue tells the story of its reinventions, the rise of the phone business, the fall, and a smaller but
more focused networks company that is growing again. Its lasting network products include the airscale radio
portfolio, the 7750 service router and FP silicon SR Linux, the 1830 optical
platforms and PSE coherent optics, fiber broadband and the research of Nokia Bell Labs. It competes with Ericson and
Huaway in mobile networks, with Cisco, Juniper and Huaway in IP routing, and with Chennai and Huaway in optical
transport. From a paper mill in 1,865 to optical and IP networks for AI data
centers, Nokia shows how a company can survive by repeatedly letting go of its past. Thanks for watching this episode of Networking Landscape.

dImcFSQdf1o.title: NVIDIA Mellanox Networking EP05
tx: In 1999, a small team of engineers in northern Israel started a chip company around a new interconnect called
Infiniband. For two decades, it was a specialist powering the world's supercomputers. Then a graphics chip
company bought it and it became the networking heart of the AI boom. This is the story of Melanox Technologies and
Nvidia networking. Infiniband and RDMA, the push into Ethernet, the $6.9 billion
acquisition, and the switches, network cards, and photonix that now connect the world's largest AI factories. We'll
follow six chapters: Melanox and Infiniband, supercomputing leadership, the move into Ethernet, the Nvidia deal,
the data center as the computer, and the AI factory era.
Melan Ox was founded in May 1999 in Yaknam, Israel by Isle Wald Man, a
former executive at the Israeli chipmaker Galileo Technology together with a group of fellow engineers. That
same year, the industry merged two competing proposals into a single new standard, Infiniband, overseen by the
Infiniband Trade Association. It was designed as a high-speed, low latency fabric to connect servers and storage.
Melon Ox bet the company on Infiniband silicon. It designed switch chips and host channel adapters, the network cards
that connect servers to an infinib fabric. Its first Infiniband chips shipped in the early 2000 under names
like Infini Scale for switches and Infini host for adapters. Many large companies that had backed infini band pulled back after the dotcom crash.
Melanox kept going, focusing on the one market where performance mattered above all, high performance computing. In
February 2007, Melanox went public on NASDAQ, raising about $12 million.
The key idea behind Infiniband is RDMA, remote direct memory access. In traditional networking, data passes
through the operating systems network stack on both ends. Every message involves the CPU, the kernel, and
several memory copies, adding latency and consuming processor cycles. With RDMA, the network adapter reads and
writes application memory directly on both servers, bypassing the kernel and the CPU. Latency drops to around a
microscond and the processors stay free for computation. For applications, sending data to another server starts to feel almost like reading local memory.
That is why RDM became the foundation for parallel computing, distributed storage and later AI training.
Infiniband also added lossless credit-based flow control and a central subnet manager. Later RDM came to
Ethernet through Rocky RDM over converged Ethernet which became essential in cloud and AI data centers.
Through the 2000s and 2010, Melanox became the standard interconnect for supercomputers. Its connect X adapters
and infin scale and later switch X and quantum switch chips moved Infini band through generation after generation of
speed from 10 Gbits per second per port to 200 Gbits. In 2011, Melanox bought
Voltater, an Israeli maker of Infini band and Ethernet switches for about $218 million, becoming a complete system
supplier rather than just a chip company. In 2013, it acquired Cotura and IPronics, adding silicon photonix and
optical components. These became the link X line of cables and transceivers.
By the early 2010, Infini Band connected a large share of the world's top 500 supercomputers, and Melon Ox had become
the clear leader in higherformance interconnects.
But supercomputing was a niche. The much bigger market was Ethernet in cloud data centers. Melanox's Connect X chips
already supported Ethernet and its 25, 50, and 100 GB Ethernet adapters became popular with cloud providers, helped by
Rocky. The bet was that the same low latency engineering that served supercomputers would matter in cloud
data centers as storage moved to flash and applications became more distributed. In 2015, Melanox launched
Spectrum, its own Ethernet switch chip and switch family, competing with Broadcombased switches. It promoted open
Ethernet, letting customers run its own operating system or alternatives such as Cumulus Linux and Sonic. In 2016, it
acquired EZ chip, a maker of network processors, which later led to the Blue Field line of data processing units. By
2019, Melanox revenue had reached about $1.3 billion.
By 2019, Melanox had attracted attention from the biggest names in computing.
Intel, Zillink, and Microsoft were all reported to be interested. On March 11, 2019, Nvidia announced it would buy
Melon Ox for about $6.9 billion in cash, Nvidia's largest acquisition at the
time. Nvidia chief executive Jensen Hong argued that the data center itself was becoming the new unit of computing and
that the network was as important as the processors. The deal needed approval from regulators in the United States,
Europe, and China. It closed on April 27, 2020 and Melanox became Nvidia
networking business with its large engineering base in Israel. Isle Waldman left Nvidia later in 2020 and the melon
ox brand was gradually retired in favor of Nvidia networking.
Inside Nvidia, the networking portfolio expanded quickly. In 2020, Nvidia also
acquired Cumulus Networks, whose Cumulus Linux network operating system gave it open software for Ethernet switches. The
same year, it launched Bluefield 2, a data processing unit or DPU, combining a network adapter with ARM processors. DPS
offload networking, storage, and security tasks from the server's main CPU. Nvidia also pitched DPS as a
security tool. isolating infrastructure software from customer workloads, an idea cloud providers were also building
into their own custom chips. Nvidia created the DOA software framework for programming DPS much as CUDA serves its
GPS. Bluefield 3 followed and in 2026, Bluefield 4 paired a 64 core Grace CPU with a Connect X9 network chip.
Alongside Melon Ox's networking, Nvidia had its own interconnect, NVLink. NVLink
debuted in 2016 with the Pascal P100GPU as a faster alternative to PCI Express
for linking GPS. In 2018, NV switch made it possible to connect 16GPS as one system in the DGX2.
In 2024, the GB200NVL72 rack linked 72 Blackwell GPUs into a
single NVLink domain. So they could work like one giant GPU. This is scale up networking. Scale up matters because
large AI models are split across many GPS that must constantly exchange data.
The larger and faster the NVLink domain, the more efficiently those GPU us work together. In 2026, NVLink 6 doubled
bandwidth again to 3.6 terabytes per second per GPU with about 260 terabytes
per second across a Vera Rubin NVL72 rack. And through NVLink Fusion, Nvidia
began licensing NVLink to other chip makers.
To connect thousands of racks, Nvidia offers two scaleout fabrics. Quantum Infiniband now at 800 Gbits per port
with Quantum X800 remains popular for the largest training clusters. And in 2023, Nvidia launched Spectrum X, an
Ethernet platform built for AI, combining Spectrum switches with Blue Field and later Connect X Super Nix
using adaptive routing and congestion control to approach Infini band performance. NVIDIA pitch was full stack
GPS network cards, switches, cables, and software designed and tuned together with reference architectures that cloud
providers could deploy quickly. Spectrum X quickly found major customers. In 2024, Nvidia said Xi's Colossus
supercomput with 100,000GPS used Spectrum X Ethernet. In 2025,
Spectrum XGS extended the platform to scale across, linking AI data centers in different locations into a single giant cluster.
As speeds climbed, the power used by optical transceivers became a major problem. NVIDIA answer was co-packaged
optics. At GTC in March 2025, Nvidia announced silicon photonix switches that
place the optical engines right next to the switch chip, eliminating most pluggable transceivers. Co-ackaging also
needs about four times fewer lasers, which Nvidia says improves reliability since lasers are among the most failureprone parts of an optical link.
At GTC 2026, Nvidia unveiled the Vera Rubin platform's networking chips.
NVLink 6, the 1.6 TBTE Connect X9 Supernick, Blue Field 4, and Spectrum 6,
a 102 4 TB Ethernet switch, and Nvidia first with co-ackaged optics. Nvidia
claims about five times better power efficiency than networks using traditional transceivers. In August
2026, Spectrum Xethernet Photonix entered full production ahead of Vera Rubin shipments.
Networking has become one of Nvidia fastest growing businesses. In the quarter ending January 2026, Nvidia
reported record networking revenue of 11 billion, up 263% from a year earlier,
