more than 8 times Melanox's entire annual revenue before the acquisition.
According to IDC, in the first quarter of 2026, Nvidia became the number one vendor in data center Ethernet switching for the
first time with 21.5% share just ahead of Arista. Vera Rubin shipments beginning in the second half
of 2026 bring all of these networking chips together in a single rack scale design. Nvidia is also moving into
telecom. In October 2025, it invested $1 billion in Nokia, taking a 2.9% stake to
build AI native radio access networks on Nvidia computing.
Nvidia networking business was built through a series of deals. Between 2011 and 2014, Melanox bought Voltater for
switch systems, Cotura and IPronics for optics, an Integrity Project for software. In 2016, EZ chip brought
network processors that led to Blue Field. And in 2020, Nvidia bought Melan Ox itself, followed by Cumulus Networks.
Over a quarter century, Infini band speed per port has grown about 80fold from 10 Gbits per second to 800 Gbits
with Quantum X800. The product lines that came out of Melon Ox, Connect X, Bluefield, Quantum, Spectrum, and LinkX
together with Nvidia, NVLink now form a complete networking stack for AI from inside the rack to across data centers.
Nvidia competes with Broadcom in switch silicon, with Arista and Cisco in Ethernet switching, and with AMD and the
ULink consortium in scaleup interconnects. From a niche supercomputing interconnect to the network of the AI factory, Melan Ox's
story shows how a long technical bet can suddenly become central to an entire industry. Thanks for watching this episode of Networking Landscape.

BOExqF2LGiQ.title: Arista Networks History EP04
tx: In 2004, three engineers started a company to build a better data center switch. Two of them had already sold a
switching startup to Cisco. 20 years later, their company had become one of Cisco's toughest competitors and the
switch maker of choice for the world's largest clouds. This is the story of Arista Networks. a single operating
system, an early bet on cloud customers, a long legal battle with Cisco, and a central role in today's AI data centers.
We'll follow six chapters. The stealth startup, winning the cloud, the IPO and the Cisco lawsuits, routing and
software, campus and branch, and the AI era.
Andy Beckall'sheim co-founded Sun Micro Systemystems and was one of the first investors in Google with David Cherry
Ton a Stanford professor. He had founded Granite Systems, a gigabit Ethernet switching company that Cisco bought in 1996.
In 2004, Beck Alheim, Cherry Ton, and engineer Ken Duda started a new company called Arastra.
Their idea was simple. The coming wave of cloud data centers would need fast programmable switches built on merchant
chips and modern software. Beck's and cherry ton funded the company themselves for years, keeping it in stealth while
the team built its software. In 2008, the company renamed itself Arista Networks and shipped its first products,
the 7100 series of 10 GB Ethernet switches. That October, Jri Ulal became
chief executive. She had spent 15 years at Cisco where she ran its data center and switching business. She would lead Arista for the next two decades.
Arista's core product has always been its software EOS, the extensible operating system. EOS runs on an
unmodified Linux kernel. Its key idea is a central state database called SISD DB.
Every process such as routing protocols or interface drivers publishes its state there and reads from it instead of talking to other processes directly.
That design means a process can crash and restart without taking down the switch. And one single software image
runs across the entire Arista hardware portfolio. So customers qualify one release instead of many. The same EOS
could also run as a virtual machine called V EOS or as a container called CEO. So engineers could build and test
entire networks in software. EOS also made programmability normal. Engineers could drop into a Linux bash shell, run
their own scripts on the switch, and control it through ei Json interface while still using a familiar industry standard command line.
Arista's timing was perfect. Cloud companies were building huge data centers with thousands of servers, and they needed a different kind of network.
Instead of the traditional three- tier design, they wanted flat leaf and spine fabrics where every server is just a few
hops from every other. Arista's fixed switches served as leaves and its modular 7500 series launched in 2010
became one of the industry's most popular spine switches. Its leaf switches such as the 750 and later the
760 series followed each new generation of Broadcom chips to market quickly moving customers from 10 to 40 and then
100 Gbit Ethernet. Its biggest customers became the companies Arista calls cloud titans, especially Microsoft and Meta.
They valued its open software, fast feature delivery, and willingness to work closely with their engineers.
Arista also won a loyal niche in financial trading where its low latency switches cut micros secondsonds out of
order execution. Customer concentration became a defining feature of Arista. For years, a handful of cloud companies have
each accounted for more than 10% of its revenue.
In June 2014, Arista went public on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker A&E. 6 months later, Cisco sued. In
December 2014, Cisco filed lawsuits claiming that Arista had copied its command line interface and infringed a
series of its patents. Many Arista executives, including Ulal, were former Cisco employees. In December 2016, a
jury found Arista not liable for copyright infringement over the command line. But at the US International Trade
Commission, Cisco won rulings on some patents, and Arista redesigned features to keep shipping its products. In August
2018, the companies settled. Arista agreed to pay Cisco $400 million. Both sides dropped their claims and they
agreed to a five-year standown from new patent suits. Arista emerged with its momentum intact. Throughout the dispute,
Arista's revenue kept growing every year, roughly doubling between 2016 and 2018.
As cloud networks grew, Arista moved beyond switching into routing. Unlike Cisco and Juniper, Arista did not design
its own packet processors. It built on merchant silicon mainly from Broadcom and competed on software system design
and speed to market. In 2016, the 7280R and 7500R series built on Broadcom's
Jericho chips with deep buffers brought internet scale routing to Arista. Its flex route technology let them hold full
internet routing tables at a fraction of the cost of traditional routers. That led to the idea of the universal spine,
one platform that could act as data center spine, data center interconnect, and peering router. The modular 7800R
series later scaled this to 400 and 800 GB Ethernet. In 2018, Arista bought
Metamakco, whose ultra- low latency devices became the 7130 series for trading firms.
Arista's second software pillar was cloud vision, launched to manage entire networks rather than individual
switches. Cloud Vision streams telemetry from every device into a central state repository built on the same principles
as EOS. Operators can see the network state at any point in time, roll back changes and automate configuration
across thousands of switches. In 2020, Arista bought big switch networks which brought its dance monitoring fabric and
awake security which added AIdriven network detection and response. Arista also open-sourced Arista validated
designs, a set of anible automation tools and introduced AVA, its autonomous virtual assist, applying AI to network
operations and security. Cloud vision later became available as a cloud service and its Wi-Fi management
inherited from Mojo became cloud vision CUE.
With its cloud business established, Arista set its sights on enterprise campus networks, Cisco's home territory.
In 2018, it bought Mojo networks for cloud managed Wi-Fi. In 2019, it
launched campus switches such as the 720 XP for power over Ethernet access running the same EOS and managed by
cloud vision. In 2022, it acquired Plurabus Networks and in July 2025, it
bought the VO cloud SDWAN business from Broadcom, giving it a complete branch offering. Its campus switches carried
data center features into the enterprise such as MAC encryption, zero-ouch provisioning, and the same automation
tools. Arista's pitch to enterprises was the same as to the clouds. one operating system, one management platform, and one
consistent architecture from the data center to the campus and branch. For 2026, it guided campus revenue to at least $1.25 billion.
Then came AI. Training large models links thousands of GPS, and the network decides whether those GPS stay busy or
sit idle. In 2023, Arista helped found the UltraEthernet Consortium to adapt Ethernet for AI and high performance
computing. Its Etherlink platforms, including 800 GB switches like the
7060X6 and the modular 7800 R4 target AI backend or scaleout networks. Arista
argued that Ethernet with its huge ecosystem and multi-endor supply would beat proprietary interconnects like
infini band for most AI clusters and hyperscalers increasingly agreed. AI networks have three layers. Scaleup
links GPS inside a rack. Scale out connects racks into one cluster and the front-end network connects the cluster
to storage and users. Arista now also targets scale across linking AI data centers over long distances and expects
to pilot Ethernet for scale up in the coming years. For 2026, Arista guided AI networking revenue to at least $3.5
billion with about 30% from scale across. AI also brought a powerful new rival.
According to IDC, Arista had been the leader in data center Ethernet switching revenue. But in the first quarter of
2026, Nvidia took the top spot for the first time with 21.5% share just ahead of Arista at about 20
7%. Across the entire Ethernet switch market, including Campus, Cisco remained the leader with about 29% while Arista
was second at about 15%. NVIDIA sells its Spectrumax switches as part of complete AI systems. Arista's answer is
openness. Its switches work with any GPU or accelerator and customers can mix vendors at every layer. Cisco,
meanwhile, is pushing its own silicon 1 systems into the same AI clusters, turning the AI data center into a three-way race.
Arista enters 2027 in the strongest position in its history. In 2025,
revenue reached $9 billion, up nearly 29%.
In the second quarter of 2026, revenue was $3 billion, up almost 38%.
After raising its outlook twice, Arista now expects 2026 revenue of about 12.6 6
billion growth of around 40% with operating margins near 50%. Next on the
road map are 1.6 TB Ethernet with volume shipments expected in 2027 and work on
new optics including co-packaged and near packaged designs. Its customer base is broadening too alongside the cloud
titans neoclouds. The specialized AI cloud providers and large enterprises are becoming more important. Though
Arista still expects at least two customers to each exceed 10% of revenue.
Unlike Cisco or Juniper, Arista grew mostly through its own engineering. Its acquisitions have been few and targeted.
In 2018, it bought Mojo Networks for Wi-Fi and Metam Makco for low latency trading. In 2020, Big Switch and Awake
Security strengthened its software for monitoring and security and Pluribus in 2022 and VO cloud in 2025 extended Arista into the campus and branch WAN.
In just over a decade as a public company, Arista grew from about half a billion in revenue to more than 12 billion expected in 2026.
Its lasting products include EOS and its single software image, cloud vision, the 7000 series switches and routers, the
universal spine and the Etherlink AI platforms. It competes with Cisco across nearly every market with Nvidia in AI
networking and with HP Juniper in data center campus and routing. From a stealth startup in 2004 to a leader of
AI networking, Arista showed that great software on merchant silicon could challenge the giants. Thanks for
watching this episode of Networking Landscape.

WcSps1HGVRk.title: Juniper Networks History EP03
tx: In 1996, a scientist from Xerox Park set out to build a router for an internet that was doubling in size every few months.
Within 3 years, his startup had broken Cisco's near monopoly in core routing and pulled off one of the most
successful IPOs of the dot era. This is the story of Juniper Networks. The routers that carried the internet's
backbone, the operating system engineers loved, the bets on security and the data center, and the AIdriven turnaround that
ended in a $14 billion sale to Huelet Packard Enterprise. We'll follow six eras. the startup years, the core router
wars, the push into security, the Ethernet and data center era, the AIdriven enterprise, and finally life inside HPE.
Prattipindu was a principal scientist at Xerox Park. He believed that routers built around generalpurpose processors
could not keep up with internet growth and that the answer was custom silicon designed for forwarding packets. He
founded Juniper in February 1996 backed by Claner Perkins. That September, Scott
Kines, a co-founder of Stratacom, became chief executive and Synindu became chief technology officer. Carriers and
equipment makers including Ericson, Lucent, Nortal, and Threecom invested $40 million. Juniper's chips were manufactured in partnership with IBM.
The operating system Jun O was released in July 1998. And in September, the first product shipped, the M40 core
router, which could forward 40 million packets per second. Inside the M40, Juniper's custom chip, the internet
processor, performed route lookups in hardware at full line rate, work that earlier routers handled largely in
software. On June 25, 1999, Juniper went public on NASDAQ at $34 a share. The
stock closed its first day up about 190%, giving the young company a market value of nearly $5 billion.
If one thing defined Juniper, it was Junos. From the start, it was designed with a clean separation between the
control plane, which computes routes, and the forwarding plane, which moves packets in hardware. Junos also changed how engineers configured networks.
Changes went into a candidate configuration and took effect only when you typed commit. Commit confirmed rolled back automatically if you locked
yourself out, and roll back restored any of the previous configurations.
Juniper promoted one operating system, one release train, and one architecture across routers, switches, and firewalls.
Later, Jun OS evolved moved the software onto a native Linux foundation. Its structured configuration and XML
interfaces made Jun OS one of the first network operating systems built for automation. Juniper engineers also
helped create Netconf the standard protocol for configuring network devices programmatically. A certification path
from JNC IA up to the expert level JNCIE built a loyal community of engineers especially in service provider networks.
In 1998, Cisco held more than 90% of the core router market. Juniper's speed and stability made it the first serious
challenger in years. Big carriers like Uunet and Cable and Wireless deployed the M40. In March 2000, the M160 arrived
about four times faster. By the end of 2000, Juniper claimed roughly a quarter of the high-end router market with Cisco
at about 70%. In 2002, the T-series followed, led by the T640, built for
terabit scale backbones. The TX matrix later linked multiple T-series chassis into a single system, a design aimed squarely at Cisco's new CRS1.
Also in 2002, Juniper bought Unisphere Networks for about $740 million, adding
the E-series broadband edge routers that connected millions of DSL subscribers.
But the dot crash hit service providers hard. Carrier spending collapsed and Juniper, like the rest of the industry, had to ride out several difficult years.
To grow beyond carriers, Juniper turned to enterprise security. In 2004, it bought Netcreen Technologies for about
$4 billion, gaining a leading line of firewall and VPN appliances and an SSLVPN business. More deals followed in 2005.
Parabit and Redline brought WAN optimization and application acceleration. Funk software brought steel belted radius, the basis for
Juniper's network access control. Not all of these lasted. The application acceleration products were later wound
down. And in 2014, Juniper sold its SSLVPN business, which became Pulse
Secure. Netcreen firewalls ran their own operating system screen OS. So in 2008,
Juniper launched the SRX series services gateways, bringing firewall, routing, and VPN together on Junos. Today, the
SRX family spans from small branch firewalls to the high-end SRX 5000 line alongside Juniper Secure Edge, a cloud-d delivered security service edge.
Security also brought one of Juniper's hardest moments. In December 2015, the company disclosed that unauthorized code
had been found in ScreenOS, which could allow encrypted VPN traffic to be decrypted. The incident made headlines
worldwide and prompted a major review of its code.
In the mid 2000s, carrier networks were moving to Ethernet. In 2006, Juniper launched the MX series, starting with
the MX960 as Ethernet edge routers for service providers. In 2009, the Trio chipset
gave the MX a programmable forwarding engine, and the MX became one of the most widely used multi-service edge
routers in the world, from broadband and business VPNs to mobile backhole. In 2008, Juniper made its biggest move into
enterprise networking. The EX series switches launched with virtual chassis, which let a stack of switches be managed
as one device. That July, Kevin Johnson, formerly of Microsoft, succeeded Scott Greens as chief executive. With Junos
running on routers, switches, and firewalls, Juniper pitched a simpler network, fewer devices to manage, and
one operating system everywhere. In 2010, Juniper bought Trapeze Networks for about $152 million, adding
Enterprise Wireless. But in campus networking, Cisco remained dominant, and Juniper's share stayed modest for years.
The boldest bet of the Johnson years was the data center. Under a project code named Stratus, Juniper spent years
designing Q Fabric, unveiled in February 2011, which aimed to make an entire data center network behave like a single
switch. Q Fabric was technically ambitious, but it was complex and customers were moving toward open scale
out leaf and spine designs. In 2013, Juniper shifted to the QFX5100
and its meta fabric architecture. In December 2012, Juniper bought Contrail
Systems for about $176 million. Contrail became Juniper's softwaredefined networking controller and its
open-source version later became Tungsten Fabric under the Linux Foundation. Also in 2011, the PTX packet
transport router arrived, designed to carry traffic across the core at lower cost. Over the next decade, the PTX
became Juniper's flagship for backbone, peering, and cloud networks. Cloud providers and content companies became
some of Juniper's most important customers, using its routers for peering and data center interconnect, and its QFX switches inside their data centers.
By 2013, growth had slowed. Kevin Johnson retired and his successor Shagan Caredpier launched an aggressive
costcutting plan under pressure from activist investor Elliot management.
Cared Pier resigned in November 2014 and Ramy Rahim who had joined Juniper in
1997 as an engineer working on the M40 became chief executive under Rahim.
Juniper focused on cloud providers and automation. It released virtual versions of its routers and firewalls, the VMX
and VSRX, and acquired App Formix for cloud monitoring, BTI systems for optical data center interconnect, and
Scyport for threat analytics. It also expanded the ACX series for mobile backhaul and cell site routing as operators began building 5G networks.
Large cloud and telecom customers remain the core of the business, but Rahim's biggest bet was still to come and it would come from Wi-Fi.
In April 2019, Juniper bought Mist systems for about $45 million.
Mist had built a cloudnative wireless platform designed from the beginning around AI and machine learning. Its
virtual network assistant, Marvis, let administrators ask questions in plain language, such as why a user's video
call was poor, and it could pinpoint the cause, whether in Wi-Fi, DHCP, DNS, or
the wired network. Mist was built on cloud microervices. So, new features shipped continuously instead of waiting
for big software releases, and its virtual Bluetooth beacons added indoor location services. Juniper extended Mist
AI from wireless to EX switches, then to the WAN and SRX firewalls and later to the data center. It called the result an
AI native networking platform. Mist transformed Juniper's enterprise business. It became one of the fastest
growing parts of the company and it put Juniper back in campus and branch deals against Cisco and Aruba.
Juniper paired Mist with a series of software acquisitions. In 2020, it bought 128 technology for about $450
million. Its session smart router offered a different approach to SDWAN routing sessions without building
traditional encrypted tunnels. In 2021, it acquired Abstra, a pioneer of intentbased data center automation that
worked across multiple switch vendors and Netrrons, whose active testing became Paragon Active assurance. For
service providers, the Paragon automation suite, now called Juniper Routing Director, brought closed loop
automation to the WAN. And in 2022, White Sand added cloud-based network access control, which became Mist access
assurance. Together, these products let Juniper offer a single operations experience driven by Mist AI from the
campus and branch to the data center and the WAN.
Through all of this, custom silicon remained Juniper's signature from the original internet processor in the M40.
The Trio family powered the MX Edge routers. The Express family powered the PTX core and cloud routers focused on
high capacity deep buffers and efficiency. Owning its silicon let Juniper tune each chip for its job. Trio
for rich edge services and per subscriber features and Express for maximum throughput per watt in the core.
In 2022, Juniper announced Express 5, a 7 nanome chip handling 28.8 8 terabs per
second and Trio 6 enabling 9 6 TB line cards for the MX10,000.
For data center switching, Juniper used merchant silicon from Broadcom in its QFX line, including 800 GB QFX switches
for AI clusters managed by AppStraw.
On January 9, 2024, Huelet Packard Enterprise announced it would buy Juniper for about $14 billion in cash or
$40 a share to combine Juniper with HP's Aruba networking business. In January
2025, the US Department of Justice sued to block the deal, arguing it would reduce competition in enterprise wireless. In June, the parties settled.
HPE agreed to sell its instant on wireless business and to license the source code of Juniper's Mist AI
operations to competitors. The acquisition closed on July 2, 2025.
Rammy Rahim took charge of HP's combined networking business, which roughly doubled in size and was expected to
contribute more than half of HP's operating income. Juniper products continue under the HPE Juniper
networking brand. In February 2026, HPE launched the PTX12000 routers built on
Express 5 with up to 518 terabs per second for connecting AI data centers.
And at Discover 2026, it introduced new QFX switches for AI clusters and announced that Marvis capabilities would come to Aruba Central.
Like Cisco, Juniper grew through acquisitions, though at a much smaller scale. In the 2000s, it bought its way into broadband, edge, security, WAN
optimization, and wireless. In the 2010s, it added softwaredefined networking, cloud monitoring, optical,
and security analytics. And from 2019, it assembled its AIdriven platform, Mist
128 technology, appstraw, Netrons, and White Sand.
Over 29 years as an independent company, Juniper grew from a single core router to a full portfolio across service
provider, cloud, and enterprise networks with revenue passing $5 billion. Its lasting product lines include Jun O, the
MT and PTX core routers, the MX edge routers, EX and QFX switches, SRX
firewalls, MS AI session smart routing, and AppStraw. It competed against Cisco from the very first day and later with
Nokia, Huawei and Arista in routing and data centers and with Aruba before joining it in the enterprise. From a bet
on custom silicon in 1996 to AI native networking inside HPE, Juniper's story
shows how a focused challenger can reshape an entire industry. Thanks for watching this episode of Networking Landscape.

nnAcd1KTk6M.title: Cisco Systems History EP02
tx: In 1984, two staff members at Stanford University started a company to sell a box that could connect different kinds
of computer networks. 42 years later, that company is a 63 billion business and its equipment carries a large share
of the world's internet traffic. This is the story of Cisco systems. The products that built it, the bets that reshaped
it, and how a router company became a platform for networking, security, observability, and now AI infrastructure. We'll move through six
eras. The router startup years, the rise of switching, the internet boom and bust, the expansion into data centers,
voice and video, the shift to software and security, and today's AI era.
The story begins on the Stanford campus in the early 1980s.
The university had a tangle of incompatible networks and staff and students built a multi-protocol router nicknamed the blue box to link them
together. Leonard Bosac, who managed the computer science department's computers, and Sandy Learner, who ran the business
schools, saw that every organization would face the same problem. In December 1984, they founded Cisco, named after
San Francisco, with a logo inspired by the Golden Gate Bridge. Their first major product, the AGS, or advanced gateway server, shipped in 1986.
It could route several protocols at once, such as TCPIP, DeckNet, Novel IPX, and Apple Talk. And that flexibility was
exactly what customers needed. In 1987, Seuia Capitals Don Valentine invested
and in 1988, John Mortgage became chief executive. On February 16, 1990, Cisco
went public on NASDAQ, valued at about $224 million. Later that year, both founders left the company.
In the early9s, Cisco turned the router into a product line. At its heart was iOS, the internet network operating
system, and its command line interface became the shared language of network engineers everywhere. The hardware
scaled in every direction. The compact 2500 series put routers into branch offices by the hundreds of thousands.
The 4,000 served regional sites and the 7,000 and later the 7,500 became the workhorses of enterprise and
internet backbones. Cisco also shaped the protocols themselves. It created IGRP and then EIGRP for routing, HSRP

tx: Welcome to episode 55, a deep dive into internet exchanges and peering. The internet is tens of thousands of independent networks. Today we look at
the places and the agreements that join them together. We'll cover transit and peering, why networks peer, private
interconnects and collocation, how an internet exchange works inside, its rules, bilateral peering and route servers, peering policies and peering
DB, route filtering with IRR and RPKI, Juno's configuration and verification, traffic engineering at the edge, CDNs,
remote peering, IXP operations and troubleshooting.
Every network on the internet is an autonomous system from episode 22 with its own AS number and its own routing policy. No single network reaches
everyone directly. Instead, networks connect to each other in two basic ways.
One network can pay another for access to the whole internet, which is transit, where two networks can agree to exchange traffic between their own customers
directly, which is peering. Almost every packet you send crosses at least one of these boundaries, where and how they happen decides the path. the latency and cost of the internet.
With transit, a customer network pays a provider, usually by bandwidth use, measured at the 95th percentile. The

provider announces the customers routes to the rest of the internet, and gives the customer routes to everywhere, often a full table of over a million IPv4 and IPv6 prefixes or simply a default route.
At the top, sit a small number of very large networks, often called tier one.
They reach the whole internet without buying transit from anyone only by peering with each other. Below them, most networks buy transit from one or more providers.
Peering is different. Two networks exchange routes for their own networks and their customers networks, but not routes they learned from other peers or
providers. So when an access ISP peers with a content provider, the ISP subscribers reach that content directly
and nothing else crosses the link. Most peering is settlement free. Neither side pays the other because both benefit roughly equally when traffic is very
unbalanced. One side may pay which is called paid peering. Remember the valley free rule from episode 22. Routes from
peers go only to customers never to other peers or providers. Break it and you've created a route leak.
Why go to the trouble of peering? Cost is the first reason. Traffic that flows over peering doesn't use paid transit.
Latency is the second. A direct path avoids detours through other networks, sometimes in other cities or countries.
Then control and resilience. You choose the path, you see problems directly with the other network, and you still have transit as a backup. For large content
and access networks, the majority of their traffic now flows over peering, not transit.
The simplest way to peer is a private network interconnect or PNI. Both networks place routers in the same building and a fiber crosscon links them porttoport often at 100 or 400 Gbits.
They run an eBGP session over that link with a small subnet like a SL31 for IPv4 and a SL127 for IPv6. A PNI gives dedicated capacity between two networks.
It makes sense when the traffic between them is large and steady. For many smaller peers, a shared exchange is far more efficient.
All of this happens in collocation facilities, buildings where many networks rent space and power for their equipment. The most valuable are carrier
neutral. Any network can come in and any network can connect to any other. Cross connects run through a meet room where the facility patches fiber between
customers cages. Because networks attract networks, a few buildings in each major city become hubs, holding hundreds of networks under one roof.
Those are exactly the buildings where internet exchanges are born.
An internet exchange point, an EXP, is a shared switching fabric that many networks connect to, so they can peer with each other without a separate cable

Route server solat. A route server is a BGP speaker run by the exchange described in RFC 7947.

Traditional networks were built like a castle with a moat. A strong firewall at the edge kept attackers out. Inside, the network was trusted. Any device on the
len or on the VPN could reach almost anything. The trouble is that one compromised laptop, one fished password
or one infected server puts an attacker inside the walls. From there, they move sideways, server to server, which is called lateral movement. Most major breaches spread exactly this way.
Meanwhile, the perimeter itself disappeared. Users work from home and coffee shops. Applications move to SAS and the public cloud. Contractors,
partners, and personal devices all need access. Traffic no longer passes through one firewall at headquarters. Being on the network is no longer a meaningful
sign of trust. So, zero trust stops treating it as one.
Zero trust is summed up as never trust, always verify. NIS described it in 2020 in special publication 800-207.
Three principles follow. Verify explicitly. Authenticate and authorize every request using identity, device health, and context. Use least
privilege. Grant only the access needed only for as long as needed. And assume breach designed so that a compromise in
one place can't spread. Notice what's missing. Network location and address on the corporate LAN earns nothing by itself.
The architecture separates deciding from enforcing. A policy enforcement point sits in front of every resource. An
access proxy, a gateway, a host agent, or a sidecar. It asks a policy decision point. Should this subject access this
resource right now? The decision point way signals who the user is, what device they're on, and its health, where and
when they're connecting, how sensitive the resource is, and any risk signals.
The answer can change midsession if the signals change.
Identity becomes the new perimeter. A central identity provider authenticates users once with single sign on and

km above the equator. At that height, a satellite circles once a day, so it appears fixed in the sky. Three satellites can cover most of the planet.
Medium Earth orbit Mio ranges from roughly 2,000 to 35,000 km, and low Earth orbit, LEO, is a few hundred to
about 2,000 km up. Alo satellite circles the earth in about 90 minutes crossing the sky in just a few.

tx: Welcome to episode 41. Every service on the internet must survive one simple threat. Someone sending it far more traffic than it can handle. That's a
distributed denial of service attack. A DD do DOS. We'll cover the kinds of attacks. Botnets reflection and amplification, sin floods, application
layer floods, and then the defenses detection, black holeing, flowspec, scrubbing centers, incast, edge protection, and a response plan.
A denial of service attack aims at availability, not secrets. The goal is simply to make a service unusable for real users. A single attacker is easy to
block. A distributed attack comes from thousands or millions of sources at once, often compromised machines. So there's no single address to filter.
Attacks are measured three ways. Bits per second, which fill links, packets per second, which exhaust routers and firewalls, and requests per second,
which exhaust applications. The largest attacks now reach several terabits per second.
DDoS attacks fall into three broad families, each aimed at a different bottleneck. Volutric attacks fill the pipe, saturating links with sheer
bandwidth. Protocol attacks exhaust state like connection tables and firewalls, load balancers and servers.
Application layer attacks send requests that look legitimate but are expensive to serve, like searches or loginins.
They need far less bandwidth and are the hardest to tell apart from real users. Many attacks combine all three.
Most attack traffic comes from buttnets, networks of compromised devices controlled by an attacker through command and control servers. In 2016,
the Murraynet infected hundreds of thousands of cameras and routers, mostly by logging in with factory default passwords and took down a major DNS
provider, making many popular sites unreachable. Today botnets also rent cloud servers and abuse residential proxies. So attack traffic can come from
ordinary home addresses and booter services sell attacks by the minute.
Reflection attacks don't send traffic to the victim directly. The attacker sends small UDP requests to public servers but
forges the source address to be the victims. The servers reply to the victim because UDP has no handshake from episode 13. The servers can't tell the
source was fake. Amplification makes it worse. A tiny request triggers a huge reply. DNS queries can amplify dozens of times. NTP monist from episode 36.
Hundreds of times. Exposed mem cacheed servers tens of thousands of times. Open services on the internet become weapons.
Reflection only works because networks let spoofed packets out. BCP 38 says every network should drop packets, leaving it with a source address it
doesn't own. An access network that assigns 203 0113/24 should never forward a packet claiming
to come from anywhere else. Uniccast reverse path forwarding automates this check. Much like the multiccast RPF check from episode 38, is the source
reachable through the interface this packet arrived on? Adoption is still incomplete, so spoofing remains possible.
The classic protocol attack targets TCP's handshake from episode 14. Bit attacker sends a flood of sins often
from spoofed addresses and never completes the handshake. The server allocates state for each halfopen connection until its backlog is full and
real clients are refused. Thin cookies fix this. Instead of storing state, the server encodes it into the sequence
number of its synak. Only when a valid app comes back does it allocate a connection. Other protocol attacks include act floods, fragment floods, and
carpet bombing which spreads traffic across a whole prefix. So no single address looks attacked.
Application layer attacks use complete valid connections. HTTP flood sends millions of real looking requests often
to expensive pages, search, login or uncashed API calls. Solaris does the opposite. It opens many connections and
sends headers very slowly tying up server workers. Protocols themselves can be abused. In 2023, the HTTP2 rapid
reset attack from episode 29 opened and immediately cancelled streams, producing record request rates from relatively small botnets.
You can't defend against what you can't see. Flow telemetry, net flow, IP fix, and S flow from episode 34. Chose
traffic per destination protocol and port detection systems learn a baseline and alert when traffic to an address jumps far beyond it or when a protocol like UDP from port 123 suddenly appears.
Good detection classifies that attack and triggers mitigation automatically within seconds because many attacks last only minutes.
The bluntest tool is black holeing. The victim's network announces that attacked address a/32 to its upstream providers
over BGP from episode 22 tagged with the black hole community 65535 666. The providers then drop all traffic
to that address at their edge before it reaches the congested link. It saves the rest of the network, but it completes the attack for that address. Nobody can reach it. It's a last resort.
Flowspec is a more precise BGP tool.
Instead of a route, it distributes firewall rules, match traffic to 198.51.10.10
from UDP source port 123 with large packets and drop it or rate limited to 10 megabits per second. Routers across
the network or upstream providers install the rule in hardware within seconds. Legitimate traffic to the same address keeps flowing. The risk. A bad
rule pushed everywhere at once can cause an outage of its own.
For large attacks, traffic is sent through a scrubbing center, a specialized network with huge capacity built to filter attacks. During an
attack, the scrubbing provider announces the victim's prefix in BGP, often a more specific/24, so all traffic flows to them. They
filter out attack traffic and return clean traffic to the origin, usually through a GRE tunnel or a direct interconnect. Service can be on demand,
diverted only during attacks or always on with traffic permanently flowing through the provider, trading some latency for instant protection.
Aniccast from episode 30 is a natural DDoS defense. When the same address is announced from hundreds of locations,
BGP sends each attacking bot to its nearest site. Abotnet spread around the world is split into hundreds of smaller attacks each absorbed locally. That's
how large CDNS DNS providers and cloud networks absorb multi-terab attacks.
Total capacity across all sites not one big pipe. The root DNS servers survive this way.
Application attacks need application aware defenses ideally at a CDN or proxy edge in front of your servers. Rate
limit per client per path. serve as much as possible from cache, so the origin never sees most requests. A web application firewall blocks known bad
patterns. Bot management scores each client using TLS fingerprints, behavior, and reputation, and can issue challenges
like a JavaScript check to suspicious clients, while real users pass straight through.
Cloud providers include basic DDoS protection for every customer at their network edge with paid tiers adding application protection response teams
and cost protection. Whatever sits in front protect the origin. If attackers find your servers real addresses, they
can go around the CDN. Allow traffic only from the provider's address ranges and don't leak origin IPs and DNS history or email headers. Autoscaling
helps absorb application floods, but it can turn an attack into a huge bill. Set limits and use stateless designs where you can, like the load balancers of episode 29.
No single tool is enough, so defenses are layered from the outside in.
Upstream providers and scrubbing absorb volutric floods. Aniccast and the CDN edge spread load and filter protocols,
rate limits, WAF rules, and bot management filter applications. and the origin is hidden and sized with headroom. Each layer handles what it's best at and passes less to the next.
When an attack starts, there's no time to figure out who to call. Write a runbook before you need it, how to confirm an attack, who decides to divert

A black hole or broadflow spec rule can block real customers too.

and application attacks hit different bottlenecks. Botnets supply the sources.
Reflection and amplification abuse spoofing and open UDP services which BCP38 with stops in cookies defeat sin

Voice became just another IP application. And 5G adds much higher speeds, lower latency, huge numbers of devices, and a cloud native core.

nodes, CNI plugins, services and Q proxy, cluster DNS, getting traffic in with load balancers, ingress and the
gateway API, network policies, egress, service meshes and ebpf.
Kubernetes runs containers and pods, groups of containers that share a network identity, and it makes a few simple promises about the network. Every
pod gets its own IP address. Every pod can reach every other pod on any node without net. And the address a pod sees
for itself is the same address others use to reach it. Kubernetes doesn't implement this itself. It defines the rules and leaves the plumbing to a
network plug-in. That separation is why there are so many ways to build a cluster network.
On a node, each pod lives in its own Linux network namespace with its own interfaces, routes, and firewall rules.
All containers in a pod share that namespace, so they reach each other on local host and must not use the same ports. A tiny pause container holds the
namespace open while app containers come and go. The pods f0 is one end of a ve pair, a virtual cable. The other end
sits in the node's root namespace, so packets leaving the pod appear on the host.
Each node gets a slice of the cluster's pod address range. Its pod cider like 10.244.1.0/24.
Between pods on the same node, traffic crosses the ve pair into the host. A bridge like CNI0 switches it at layer 2
or the host routes it at layer 3 with one route per pod. Either way, it goes straight to the other pods ve without leaving the machine.
across nodes. The network underneath doesn't know about pod addresses. There are two main answers. An overlay wraps each pod packet in an outer packet
between node addresses, usually vxlan from episode 23 or jeneive. It works on any network, but adds headers and lowers the MTU typically from 1500 to 1450.
Native routing advertises each node's pod cireer to the network often with BGP from episode 22 or programs the cloud's
route tables. Packets travel unwrapped with full MTU and are easier to trace but the network must cooperate.
The glue is CNI the container network interface a simple specification for network plugins. When the cubullet
starts a pod the container runtime calls the CNI plugin with an add command. The plug-in creates the ve pair, assigns an
address through IPAM, IP address management, and sets up routes. When the pod is deleted, the EL cleans up.

interfaces and addresses which caps pods per node. Plan subnets with room to grow or use prefix delegation.
Pods are disposable. They're replaced on every deploy and come back with new addresses. Clients need something stable. A service gives a set of pods,
one stable virtual IP, the cluster IP like 10.96.12.40 and a DNS name. A label selector like app equals web picks the pods.

Cluster IPs only work inside the cluster to reach a service from outside. There are other service types. A node port

external traffic policy to local only uses pods on the receiving node and preserves the client IP.
One load balancer per service gets expensive for HTTP. A single entry point can route by host and path. An ingress resource describes those rules.

tx: Welcome to episode 37. So far, we've looked inside data centers and the cloud. Today, we look at how an enterprise connects everything else,
branch offices, stores, factories, and people working from anywhere. That's the world of SDW and Sassy. We'll see why
the classic W broke down, how SDWAN builds an overlay across any kind of link, how it routes each application on
the best path, and how Sassy moves security into the cloud with zero trust access replacing the old VPN.
The traditional enterprise WN was hub and spoke. Every branch had a private MLS circuit from episode 26 back to the
headquarters or data center. Internet traffic from branches was backhauled over MLS to the data center and sent out through one central set of firewalls. It
was predictable and secure but expensive. New circuits took weeks or months to install and bandwidth was costly.
Then applications moved. Email, office suites, CRM and video calls became SAS hosted in the cloud not in the data
center. Back hauling the traffic branch in Denver reached a SAS service in Denver by way of a data center in Virginia. The airbin added latency and
filled expensive MLS links. Meanwhile, broadband and 5G became fast and cheap.
Enterprises wanted to use them without losing control or security.
SDWAN softwaredefined WN builds an overlay on top of whatever transports a site has. MLS, broadband, LTE or 5G. An
edge device at each site builds encrypted tunnels, usually IPS SEC from episode 27 over every transport to the
other sites and hubs. Then a central brain decides for each application which tunnel to use. The transports become interchangeable pipes and policy lives above them.
SDWAN has three layers much like the networks we've seen before. The orchestrator is the management plane,
the portal where you define sites, templates, and policies. The controller is the control plane. It distributes routes, keys, and policies to every
edge. And the edges are the data plane, forwarding packets. Because control is centralized, a policy change like
prioritizing a new video app reaches thousands of sites in minutes.
Deploying a new branch used to need a skilled engineer on site. With zero touch provisioning, the box is shipped to the store. Someone plugs in power and
an internet cable. The edge gets an address by DHCP, calls home to a known cloud address, proves its identity with
a certificate, and downloads its configuration. Minutes later, the site is part of the overlay combined with broadband or 5G. A branch can be online the day it opens.
The overlay can take several shapes. Hub and spoke sends everything through regional hubs. Full Mesh builds tunnels between every pair of sites to branchto
branch traffic like voice calls goes direct. Many designs mix the two with dynamic tunnels created on demand. Every
tunnel is constantly probed so the edge always knows the current latency, jitter and loss on every path.
This is the heart of SDW routing by application and by path quality not just by destination. Each
application class gets an SLA. Voice, for example, might require latency under 150 milliseconds, jitter under 30, and
loss under 1%. When the broadband paths loss climbs to 3%, voice moves to the MLS path within a second, while bulk
traffic stays where it is. When broadband recovers, voice can move back to route by application. The edge must
know what each flow is. It uses D packet inspection, TLS server names, DNS answers, and known address ranges of SAS
providers, often from the very first packets of a flow. Then policies follow intent. Voice prefers MLS. Office apps
break out locally to the internet and backups use the cheapest broadband link at low priority.
SDWAN can also hide bad links. With active active links, traffic is spread across all transports and a failure
moves flows in under a second. Forward error correction sends extra parity packets so lost packets can be rebuilt at the far end. And packet duplication
sends critical traffic like a voice call over two paths at once. The far edge keeps whichever copy arrives first.
With local internet breakout, SAS traffic leaves directly from the branch with no hairpin through the data center.
performance improves dramatically. But now every branch is an internet edge.
Where do the firewalls, web filtering, and thread inspection happen? Putting a full security stack in every store is expensive and hard to manage. That problem is what sassy solves.
Sassy, secure access service edge, a term coined by Gartner in 2019, combines SDWA and networking with security services delivered from the cloud.
Instead of central firewalls, a provider runs a global network of points of presence. Branches and users connect to the nearest one and inspection happens
there close to the user. The security half on its own is often called as SE security service hedge.
SSE bundles several services. A secure web gateway filters web traffic, blocks malware, and enforces acceptable use. A
CASBY cloud access security broker controls which SAS apps are used and how. Firewall as a service applies network policy to all other traffic.
Data loss prevention watches for sensitive data leaving and ZTNA zero trust network access replaces the remote access VPN.
A traditional VPN puts the user on the network. Once connected, they can often reach far more than they need. ZTNA
grants access to one application at a time. After checking the user's identity and the devices health, like disk encryption and patches, everything else
stays invisible. The application itself is hidden, too. A small connector next to it makes an outbound connection to the broker, so nothing listens on the internet for attackers to scan.
How does traffic reach the sassy cloud?
Branches send it through IPSC or Gre tunnels to the nearest point of presence. Remote users run a lightweight agent which tunnels their traffic to.

SDWAN extends into public clouds, too. A virtual edge runs inside a VPC or connects to a cloud transit gateway. So
branches reach cloud workloads over the same overlay and policies. Some providers also offer a private middle mile. Traffic enters their backbone near
the branch and leaves near the cloud region, avoiding the unpredictable public internet in between.
Most enterprises migrate gradually.
Start with dual transports at each site, often keeping a smaller MLS circuit alongside broadband. carry segmentation end to end with separate VRFS for
corporate guest and payment traffic. And remember QoS from episode 25. The overlay can prioritize inside tunnels,
but the underlay must also honor the markings or shape below the link speed, so cues build where you control them.
SDW gives operators far more visibility than a classic W. Dashboards show each application's experience at each site,
latency, loss, and which path it took, minuteby minute. Brown outs where a lake is up but degraded finally become visible. Sassy adds user level insight.

clock off by 20 parts per million gains or loses about 1.7 seconds every day.
Temperature changes the rate, too. So a clock left alone drifts further and further. It needs to be disciplined compared against a better reference again and again with its rate corrected.
The best references are atomic clocks which define the second itself. Most networks get atomic time from satellites. GPSo
and other GNSS systems broadcast time from atomic clocks on board and a receiver with a roof antenna can recover it to within tens of nanconds. A GNSS
receiver often built into a dedicated time server becomes the reference for the whole network.

IP packets carry a TTL from episode 11, so a routing loop eventually ends.
Ethernet frames have no TTL. A frame in a loop circulates forever. Worse, switches flood broadcasts out of every
port. In a loop, each copy is flooded again and again. Within seconds, a broadcast storm fills every link and
switch CPUs max out. MAC address tables flap as the same source address appears on different ports and hosts receive
duplicate frames. The network grinds to a halt. Yet we still want redundant links.
The answer invented by radio Pearlman in 1985 is the spanning tree protocol standardized as a E82.1D.
Twitches cooperate to pick a loop-f free tree that reaches every segment. The extra links aren't removed. Their ports are blocked ready to take over if an
active link fails. Physically, the network has loops. Logically, frames only ever follow the tree.
Fitch's exchange bridge protocol data units or BPD bus sent every two seconds to the multiccast address 0180 C2 000 0 0 0.

bridge ID is a priority plus a MAC address. The priority defaults the 32768 set in steps of 4096 and in per VLAN
versions includes the VLAN number. The lowest bridge ID wins.

depends on link speed. In the long method, a 1 GB link costs 20,000 and a 10 GB link costs 2,000. On every

link between switch two and switch three. Both have the same cost to the route. So the tie is broken by bridge ID. Switch 2's ID is lower. So its port

Classic 802.1D is cautious. A port moves from blocking to listening for 15 seconds to learning for another 15 and
