tx: Welcome to episode 4. Last time we stayed inside the local network. Now we leave layer 2 behind and look at how
routers find paths across networks. This is the routing deep dive. We'll cover how routers choose routes, OPF and its
areas, BGP and its path selection, traffic engineering, redistribution, routing security, and fast convergence.
Here is our lab, an enterprise network with its own autonomous system number AS-64,496.
Inside it runs OPF, the backbone area 0 connects rowers R1, R2 and R3, and the
two edge rowers E1 and E2. Branch sites sit in area 1 and area 2 connected through R1 and R3. At the edge, E1 and
E2 run BGP with two internet providers, ISPA and AS64,500 and ISPB and AS64,510.
Our public prefix is 198.51.100.0/24.
Before we dive into protocols, let's recall how our router chooses a route. There are three rules applied in order.
First, longest prefix match for a packet to 10.1.4.7, 4.7 A /24 route beats a SL16 which beats the default route.
Second, if different sources offer the same prefix, the router trusts the one with the lowest administrative distance.
On Cisco routers, connected is zero, static is one, EBGP is 20, OPF is 110, and IBGP is 200. Third, within one
protocol, the lowest metric wins, such as the lowest OPF cost. And if several paths tie on metric, the router can install all of them and share traffic
across them. That's equal cost multipath or ECMP.
Routing happens in two planes. In the control plane, protocols like OPF and BGP each pick their best routes and offer them to the routing information
base or RIB. The RIB chooses the winners. The winners are programmed into the forwarding information base or FIB inside the router's hardware along with
the next top MAC address. Packets are then forwarded by the fib at line rate without the control plane ever touching them.
Routing protocols come in two main families. Distance vector protocols like RIP share their routing tables with their neighbors. I can reach this
network in this many hops. Each router only knows what its neighbors tell it which is often called routing by rumor.
They converge slowly and can suffer from count to infinity loops rip limits paths to 15 hops. For this reason, link state
protocols like OPF and ISIS isis work differently. Every router floods a description of its own links to every
other router. So, every router builds the same complete map of the network and calculates its own shortest paths using Dystra's algorithm.
OPF open shortest path first is the most common interior routing protocol in enterprises. It runs directly over IP as
protocol number 89. Routers discover neighbors by sending hello packets to the multiccast address 224.0.0.5
every 10 seconds by default. If no hello arrives for 40 seconds, the neighbor is declared dead. To become neighbors, both
sides must agree on the area, the subnet and mask. The hello and dead timers and authentication. A mismatched MTU will also stall the database exchange.
Neighbors move through a series of states down in it two-way exart exchange loading and finally full when their databases are synchronized.
Every OPF router has a router ID, a 32-bit number written like an IP address. It's usually set by hand such as 1.1.1.1
so it stays stable and easy to read. On shared segments like Ethernet, routers elect a designated router, the DR, and a
backup designated router, the BDR, to cut down on flooding. Other routers form full agencies only with the DR and BDR
instead of with every other router. With 10 routers, that's 17 adjacencies instead of 45. The highest OPF priority
wins the election with the highest router ID as the tiebreaker. On pointto-point links, there's no election at all.
Each OPF link has a cost. By default, the cost is a reference bandwidth of 100 megabits divided by the interface
bandwidth. That old default makes 100 megbit, 1 GB, and 10 GB links all cost one. So, modern networks raise the
reference bandwidth, for example, to 100 Gbits. Each router then runs Dystra's shortest path first algorithm over its link state database. Starting from
itself, it repeatedly adds the closest router that's not yet in the tree until every router has its lowest total cost path. The result is a shortest path tree
and best routes go into the routing table. Equal cost paths can all be installed free CMP.
In a large network, flooding every change to every router and running SPF everywhere doesn't scale. So, OPF splits
the network into areas. Area zero is the backbone and every other area must connect to it. Routers with interfaces in two areas are called area border
routers or a BRS. In our lab, R1 and R3 are a BRS. Detailed topology stays inside each area. Other areas see only
summary routes. So, a link flapping in area 1 doesn't make the routers in area 2 rerun SPF.
OSPF describes the network using link state advertisements or LS as here are the main types. Type one router LSS
describe each router's own links. Type two network LSS are created by the DNR for shared segment. Both stay inside
their area. Type three summary LSS are created by ABRS to advertise networks from one area into another. Type five
external LSS carry routes redistributed from outside OPF created by an autonomous system boundary rotor or
ASBR. Type four tells other areas how to reach that SBR. In our lab, the edge router Z1 and E2 are SBS because they
inject the default route from the internet.
Areas can be trimmed even further. A stub area blocks type five external routes and gets a default route instead.
A totally stubby area also blocks type three summaries, so its routers see little more than a default route. A not so stubby area or NSSA is a stub area
that still needs to import some external routes. It carries them as type 7 LSS which the ABR converts to type five and
a BRS can summarize if area 1 uses the subnets 10.1.0.0 through 10.1.255.0
the IB advertises just 10.1.0.0/16 keeping routing tables small and stable
inside our network OPF finds the best paths between networks. The internet uses BGP the border gateway protocol
version 4. BGP is a path vector protocol. Each route carries the list of autonomous systems it has crossed called
the VS path. BGP routers called peers connect over TCP port 179. A session moves from idle through connect and
active then open sent and open confirm to established. Sessions between different autonomous systems are external BGP or EBGP. Sessions inside
the same autonomous system are internal BGP or IBGP. In our lab, E1 peers with ISPA, E2 peers with ISPB and E1 and E2 peer with each other over IBGP.
BGP peers exchange four types of message. Open to start a session, keep a live to keep it up, update to announce or withdraws, and notification to report
an error and close the session. Each update carries path attributes such as the AS path, the next hop, the origin, local preference, med and communities.
The AS path also prevents loops. If a router sees its own S number in an incoming path, it rejects the route. BGP
is incremental. After the initial exchange, peers only send changes, which matters when the full internet table holds over a million routes.
IBGP has a special rule. A route learned from one iBGP pier is not passed on to another IBGP pier. That prevents loops
inside the as but it means every iBGP router must peer with every other one with 50 routers. That's 1,225 sessions.
Route reflectors solve this. Clients peer only with a reflector which is allowed to pass routes between them. One more detail. Routes from EBGP keep the
external next hop. Edge routers usually set next hop self so internal routers can reach the next hop through OPF.
When BGP has several paths to the same prefix, it picks one best path using a fixed list of tiebreers. First, the next
hop must be reachable. Then it prefers the highest weight which is local to Cisco routers and then the highest local preference which is shared across the
whole AS. Next, it prefers routes this router originated, then the shortest AS path, then the lowest origin type, and
then the lowest MED. After that, it prefers EBGP over IBGP paths, then the closest exit by IGP metric, and finally the oldest path or the lowest router ID.
You don't need to memorize every step on day one. Local preference and SP path length decide most real world choices.
Let's see it work. Our lab learns the prefix 203.0.13. 0.113.0/24 from both providers. From ISPA, the ASP
Weight and local preference are equal.
So, the shortest AS path wins. Two hops through ISPIA beats three hops through ISPB. But suppose ISPB is our faster,
cheaper link. We set local preference 200 on routes from ISPB. Local preference is checked before AS path. So now all outbound traffic prefers ISPB
because local preference is shared over IBGP. E1 learns it too and sends its traffic across to E2.
Local preference controls how traffic leaves our network. Controlling how traffic comes in is harder because other networks make their own choices. The most common tool is AS path prepending.
We announce our prefix to ISP head with our AS number repeated so that path looks longer and the rest of the internet prefers ISPB. Med can suggest a
preferred entry point to a neighbor that has several links to us and BGP communities. Let us ask our provider to apply policies for us. Announcing a more
specific prefix also attracts traffic because longest prefix match always wins, but it adds routes to the global table. So use it with care.
Real networks run more than one routing source. Route redistribution copies routes from one source into another.
Common examples are redistributing static or connected routes into OPF, injecting a default route into OPF at the edge, and advertising internal
prefixes into BGP. Each protocol measures distance differently, so redistributed routes need a seed metric.
In OPF, they appear as external type 2 routes by default, keeping the same cost everywhere. In our lab, E1 and E2
originate a default route into OPF. So every internal router knows the way out.
Redistribution is powerful, but it's one of the most common sources of routing loops. With two redistribution points, a route can go from protocol A into
protocol B on one router and back from B into A on the other. Now it's circulating with misleading metrics.
Administrative distance can also make a router prefer the redistributed copy over the original route. The fixes redistribute as little as possible. Tag
routes when you redistribute them and filter tagged routes so they never come back. Route maps and prefix lists do this job.
Route maps and prefix lists are the main policy tools. A prefix list matches prefixes and lengths. For example,
10.1.0.0/16LE24 matches that network and any subnet of it up to/24. A route map is an ordered
list of match and set rules. Match these routes. Then set local preference, tags, communities or metrics or deny them. At
the internet edge, filtering is also security. Announce only your own prefixes. Set a maximum prefix limit on each session and drop bugons addresses
that should never appear on the internet. And use RPKI route origin validation to reject routes announced by the RON as which protects against many hijacks and leaks.
How fast does routing recover from a failure? It depends on how quickly the failure is detected. BGP's default hold time is 180 seconds on many routers and OPF's dead interval is 40 seconds.
That's far too slow for modern applications. BFD birectional forwarding detection sends tiny hoss every few
hundred milliseconds or faster and tells OPF and BGP within a second when a path goes down. Faster route goes further.
Loop-free alternate paths are precomputed and installed in hardware so traffic can switch to a backup path in under 50 milliseconds before the protocols even recon converge.
When a routing breaks start with the neighbors an OPF neighbor that never appears often means mismatched hello
timers area IDs subnet masks or authentication succinct start or exchange usually means an MTU mismatch.
ABGP session stuck inactive means TCP 179 isn't connecting. Check the neighbor address, the remote AS number,
firewalls, and for loop back peering, the update source and EBGP multihop. If the session is established but routes are missing, check your filters, next
hop reachability, and whether the route is in the BGP table at all. And for unexpected paths, compare administrative distances and metrics and walk through the BGP decision process step by step.
These are the commands you'll use most, shown in common router syntax. Show iposp neighbor shows each neighbor at its state. Show ip route lists OPF
routes. O for interaria, o i if for interaria and o e2 for external. Show ipgp summary shows every session at how
many prefixes each pier sent. Show ipbgp for prefix shows every path and marks the best one with a greater than sign.
And trace route confirms the path the packets really take. Let's recap the routing deep dive.
Routers choose the longest prefix first, then the lowest administrative distance, then the best metric. The RIB picks the routes and the fib forwards in hardware.
OPF is link state, neighbors, lss, SPF and areas with a BRS and summaries to scale. BGP connects autonomous systems
using path attributes and policy. Local preference steers outbound traffic, propending steers inbound traffic and redistribution needs careful filtering.
In the next episode, we go into the data center spine and leaf fabrics ECMP and VXLAN with EVPN. See you there.

3fO32oxrJEk.title: Switching Deep Dive
tx: Welcome to episode 3. Last time we followed a packet across many networks.
Now we zoom into the place where most packets start and end, the switched local network. This is the switching deep dive. We'll cover how switches
really work. VLANs and trunks, routing between VLANs, spanning tree, link aggregation, layer 2 security, and campus design.
Here is our lab. A small campus network.
Two distribution switches, DSW1 and DSW2, connect to the firewall and the internet. Their layer three switches, so
they also route between VLANs. Two access switches, ISW1 and ASW2, connect the users. Each access switch has an uplink to both distribution switches.
For redundancy, we'll use three VLANs.
VLAN 10 for staff on 1010.0/24, VLAN 20 for voice on 1010.20.0/24, 0/24 and VLAN 34 guests on 1010.30.0/24.
Let's start with what a switch does with every frame. It has three jobs, learn, forward, and flood. Learning. The switch reads the source MAC address of each
incoming frame and records the port it arrived on in its MAC address table.
Forwarding, it looks up the destination MAC. If it's known, the frame goes out only that one port. If the destination is on the same port the frame came from, the frame is filtered and dropped.
Flooding. If the destination is unknown or it's a broadcast, the frame is sent out every port except the one it came in on. Entries age out after 300 seconds of
silence by default, so the table stays current as devices move.
Inside a modern switch, all of this happens in hardware at line rate on every port at once. The MAC table lies in a special memory called CAM which finds an exact match in a single lookup.
Access lists and quality of service rules use TCAM which can also match patterns with wild cards. Switches forward in one of two ways. Door and
forward receives the whole frame and checks the FCS before sending it. Cutth through starts sending as soon as it reads the destination address which
lowers latency. Broadcasts, unknown uniccasts, and multiccasts are all flooded together. They're called bum traffic and controlling it is a big part of switch design.
Here's the problem with one big flat network. Every broadcast reaches every device. ARP requests, DHCP discovers,
and other chatty protocols all flood the whole network with hundreds of devices.
That's a lot of noise. There's also no separation. Guest laptops sit on the same network as staff computers and phones. We could buy separate switches
for each group, but there's a much better answer. Virtual LANs.
A VLAN splits one physical switch into several logical switches. Each VLAN is its own broadcast domain. A broadcast in
VLAN 10 never reaches VLAN 20 or VLAN 30. In practice, each VLAN gets its own IP subnet. One VLAN, one subnet is the
rule to remember. Ports that connect to end devices are access ports. Each access port belongs to exactly one VLAN.
And the device never even knows VLANs exist.
So, how does VLAN information travel between switches? Through trunk links. A trunk carries many VLANs over one cable to keep them apart. The switch inserts a
four byte tag into each frame defined by the ITLE E82.1Q standard. The tag sits between the source MAC address and the
ether type. It starts with the value hex 8100 which says a tag follows. Then come three bits of priority used for quality
of service. One drop eligible bit and a 12 bit VLAN ID. 12 bits allow 4,96
values 0 and 4,95 are reserved. So you can use VLANs 1 to 494.
Let's follow a frame across a trunk. A staff PC on ASW1 sends a normal untagged frame into its access port in VLAN 10.
ASW1 adds a tag for VLAN 10 and sends the frame up the trunk. DSW1 reads the tag and knows exactly which VLAN the
frame belongs to. When the frame leaves an access port on the far side, the tag is removed. End devices only ever see
untagged frames. One VLAN on a trunk is special. The native VLAN whose frames are sent untagged. Both ends must agree
on it. And it's good practice to set it to an unused VLAN.
Here's how this looks on a typical switch command line. For an access port, you set the mode to access and assign the VLAN. For an IP phone with a PC
plugged in behind it, you can add a separate voice VLAN. For a trunk, you set the mode to trunk. Choose the native VLAN and limit the allowed VLANs to only the ones that need to cross that link.
Then verify with show VLAN brief and show interface is trunk.
VLANs keep traffic apart, but staff still need to reach servers and the internet and moving traffic between VLANs needs routing. The classic way is
router on a stick. One router link is a trunk split into sub interfaces, one per VLAN, each holding the gateway address for that subnet. A packet from VLAN 10
to VLAN 20 goes up the trunk to the router, gets routed, and comes back down the same cable tagged for VLAN 20. It
works, but that single link quickly becomes a bottleneck.
Today, most networks route between VLANs on a layer 3 switch instead. Each VLAN gets a switched virtual interface or
SVI, a virtual router port inside the switch that holds the gateway address such as 10.10.1 for VLAN 10. The switch routes between
VLANs and hardware at full speed with no hairpin through an external router. For redundancy, both distribution switches
share one virtual gateway address using a first top redundancy protocol such as VRRP or HSRP. If one switch fails, the other takes over.
Now, redundancy. We connected each access switch to both distribution switches. So, one failure can't cut users off, but that creates a loop.
Ethernet frames have no time to live. A broadcast sent into a loop circles forever and every switch floods it again. So the copies multiply within seconds. This becomes a broadcast storm.
Links fill up. Switch CPS max out and MAC tables flap as the same address appears on different ports. The whole network can go down. We need redundant
links without loops. And that is the job of the spanning tree protocol.
Banning tree defined in ITLE E82.1D turns a loop network into a loop-f free tree by blocking just enough ports.
Twitches exchange messages called BPDOS bridge protocol data units. The first step is electing a root bridge. Every
switch has a bridge ID, a priority 32,768 by default, followed by its MAC address.
The lowest bridge ID wins. If all priorities are equal, the lowest MAC wins, which is often the oldest switch in the building. That's why you set the
priority yourself and make your best distribution switch the route.
Next, every other switch finds its best path to the route using path cost.
Faster links cost less. For example, four for 1 GB and two for 10 GB. Each non-root switch picks one root port, the
port with the lowest total cost to the route. On each link, one designated port is chosen to forward traffic onto that link. Every port on the root bridge is
designated. Any port left over becomes an alternate port and is blocked. In our campus, the uplinks from the access switches to DSW2 are blocked and the
loops are gone. If an active uplink fails, spanning tree unblocks the alternate port and traffic flows again.
Classic spanning tree was careful and slow. After a failure, a blocked port could wait up to 20 seconds of max age, then move through the listening and
learning states, spending 15 seconds of forward delay in each before it could forward. So recovery could take 30 to 50 seconds. That's an eternity for voice calls and applications.
Rapid spanning tree it e2.1 fixed this and it's the default on most switches today. Twitches negotiate
directly with a proposal and agreement handshake instead of waiting for timers and alternate ports are pre-calculated as instant backups. Convergence drops
from tens of seconds to usually under a second. Ports that connect end devices should be edge ports called portf fast on Cisco switches. They go straight to
forwarding and BPDU guard shuts down an edge port if a BPDU ever arrives protecting the network from someone plugging in a rogue switch.
There are a few spanning tree flavors per VLAN versions such as PVST plus run a separate tree for every VLAN. Multiple
spanning tree or MSTP maps many VLANs onto a few instances which scales much better with separate trees. You can make
DSW1 the route for VLAN 10 and DSW2 the route for VLAN 20. So both up links carry traffic. That's simple load
sharing. Even so every blocked link is wasted bandwidth. That's where link aggregation comes in.
Link aggregation combines several physical links into one logical link called a poor channel or a lag. Banning tree sees the bundle as a single port.
So nothing is blocked and every link carries traffic. If one member fails, traffic shifts to the others in milliseconds. The bundle is negotiated
by LACP. The link aggregation control protocol from E82.3 A now 802.1 AX. Both sides must agree on speed and settings.
A typical bundle has two, four, or eight links.
But how does a switch spread traffic across the links? It doesn't split frames. Instead, it uses a hash. The switch takes fields like the MAC
addresses, IP addresses, and ports. Runs them through a hash function and picks a member link. Every packet of one flow
takes the same link, so packets never arrive out of order. The catch, a single flow can never go faster than one member link. Four 10 GB links give 40 GBs in
total, but one big transfer still tops out at 10.
Normally a bundle must end on a single switch but that switch is then a single point of failure. Multi- chassis link aggregation or Mlag lets two switches
act as one LACP partner. Cisco calls this VPC and other vendors use similar names. Now ASW1 bundles one link to DSW1
and one to DSW2 into a single port channel. Both links are active, nothing is blocked and either distribution switch can fail. Banning tree still runs
as a safety net, but in a well-built ML lag design, it has nothing to block.
Layer 2 is a common target for attacks, so switches include several protections.
Port security limits how many MAC addresses can appear on a port to stop MAC flooding attacks that overflow the MAC table. DHCP sweeping only trusts
DHCP replies from uplink ports, so a rod DHCP server can't hand out a fake gateway. It also records which device
has which address. Dynamic AARP inspection uses that record to drop forged ARP replies which blocks ARP spoofing and man-in-the-middle attacks.
802.1x makes devices authenticate before the port opens at all and can place each one into the right VLAN automatically
and storm control rate limits broadcast and multiccast traffic as a last line of defense against storms.
Let's zoom out to campus design. The traditional model has three layers.
access switches for users, distribution switches that aggregate and route between VLANs, and a core for fast transport between buildings. Smaller
sites often use a collapsed core, where distribution and core are the same pair of switches. Just like our lab, access switches usually provide power over
Ethernet, powering phones, cameras, and access points through the data cable.
The newest standard delivers up to 90 watts per port.
Newer designs shrink layer 2 even further. In routed access, every access switch is also a layer three router. So there are no layer 2 loops between
switches and spanning tree is almost nothing to do. Campus fabrics use EVPN and VXLAN, the same overlays we met in
data centers to stretch a VLAN anywhere while the underlay stays fully routed.
The lesson is simple. Keep layer 2 domain small and route as early as you can.
When switching goes wrong, the same problems appear again and again. A device in the wrong VLAN gets the wrong subnet or no address at all. Check the
port with show VLAN brief. A VLAN that isn't allowed on a trunk works on one switch but not across the link. Check
show interfaces trunk. A native VLAN mismatch can leak traffic between VLANs and a port that suddenly goes dark may
be error disabled by BPDU guard or port security. Finally, a slow network with flapping MAC addresses and high CPU usually means a loop.
Here are the commands you'll use most shown in common switch syntax. Joe MAC address table finds the port a device is on and show vlan brief lists each VLAN
and its access ports. Joe spanning tree reveals the root bridge and each port's role and state and show ether channel summary confirms that bundles are up on
Linux hosts and white box switches. The bridge and IP link commands show the same ideas. Let's recap the switching deep dive.
Switches learn source MAC addresses, forward known destinations, and flood the rest. VLANs split a switch into separate broadcast domains, one subnet
each. Trunks carry many VLANs using 802.1 Q tags and layer 3 switches route between VLANs with SV. It is vanning
tree blocks loops. Rapid spanning tree makes recovery fast and link aggregation with LACP and Mlag puts every link to work. In the next episode, we leave
layer 2 behind for the routing deep dive. OPF areas, BGP path selection and route redistribution. See you there.
